docs.title: SLEvolve v1.0
docs.text: SLEvolve was developed by Xiyuan Bao. It combines an exact recursive reformulation of the viscoelastic memory, engineering optimizations of the solver, and physics-inspired iteration starts; the implementation was AI-agent-assisted, with the formulation, the algorithms and the acceptance criteria set by the author and every change verified against the legacy solver.

docs.title: What SLEvolve solves
docs.text: SLEvolve solves the gravitationally self-consistent sea-level equation on a spherically symmetric viscoelastic Earth, including shoreline migration, marine ice grounding, rotational feedback and the outer iteration on the initial topography of ice age runs. The explicit load-history sum of the pseudo-spectral formulation is replaced by an exact recursive modal state, so the cost per time step does not grow with the length of the load history and the total cost grows as O(N) instead of O(N^2) in the number of time steps N. A Fortran solver derived from the legacy code of Han et al. (2022) and a Python solver written from scratch give results identical to round-off (below 1e-11 m in the three benchmark cases).

docs.title: Install and first run
docs.text:
Get the code:

git clone https://github.com/xiyuanbao/slevolve && cd slevolve

Python (no install step; the quick start runs the Python solver):

conda create -n slevolve -c conda-forge python=3.12 numpy numba ducc0 scipy netcdf4 matplotlib
conda activate slevolve
python examples/quickstart.py

Fortran (build, then the Fortran test, which also needs the Python env above for the comparison):

conda create -n slevolve-fortran -c conda-forge gfortran fftw openblas llvm-openmp
conda activate slevolve-fortran
CASE=case1 bash fortran/build.sh            # last line: built: .../fortran/build/case1/exe (...)
PYTHON="$(conda run -n slevolve which python)" bash tests/test_fortran_python.sh   # prints PASS

Fortran only (no Python at all; toolchain from conda, Homebrew or apt, see Fortran without Python):

bash tests/test_fortran_synthetic.sh        # builds, generates the synthetic Earth in Fortran, prints PASS

docs.title: Running the benchmark cases
docs.text:
This page gives the input preparation and run commands of the three benchmark cases for both solvers.

Data provenance, the corrupt Earth-model file of Case 2 and the total-versus-grounded ice issue of Case 1 are documented in Benchmark provenance. The scripts in examples/ contain the commands below; each takes the prepared INPUT_FILES directory from the environment variable INPUT and the thread count from THREADS (default 8), builds the Fortran executable with the matching CASE preset (into fortran/build/<case>/) and runs in the current directory. The Fortran build uses the active toolchain (Installation); set CONDA_ENV=slevolve-fortran instead of activating it, if you prefer. The Python commands need the Python environment of the same page.

Summary (wall times of the Python reference runs on an Apple M4 Max with 8 threads):

case run Python wall time memory and disk 1 forward run, 550 x 1 yr 20 s 2.2 GB of ice input (.bin); every output field is 4 MB per step, so restrict the steps (SLEVOLVE_SNAP) or fields (--save-fields) 2 one outer pass, 1200 x 200 yr 38 s ice cache of about 5 GB in python/cache/ (Python) 3 first-pass topography 13 s + 5 outer passes 18 s 31 s 0.5 GB of ice input (text)

docs.title: Case 1: Antarctic forward run (550 × 1 yr)
docs.text:
Data (about 9 GB to download):

  • Dryad, Yousefi et al. (2022), doi:10.5061/dryad.ncjsxkswm: fort.92_85_MISI.nc.xz (8.9 GB; decompress with xz -d), the ice thickness of the ice-sheet run.
  • OSF, Han et al. (2022), doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/8PTFM, folder Data/AIS_550yr/: INPUT_AIS history.zip (127 MB; the archived grounded-ice files AISload_gd_Run85_0_0_0 .. _550; unzip it with unzip "INPUT_AIS history.zip", quoting the name because of the space), INPUT_Others/prem_512.l60K2C.sum18p6.dum19p2.tz19p4.lm22 (also shipped in lovenum/), and from OUTPUTS_StandardSimulations.zip (2.0 GB) only the member OUTPUTS_StandardSimulations/dt=1yr/topo0 (unzip -j OUTPUTS_StandardSimulations.zip 'OUTPUTS_StandardSimulations/dt=1yr/topo0'), saved as topo0_archive.

Input tree (/path/to/INPUT_FILES)

  • icemodel/AISload_gd_Run85_0_0_<k>.bin, k = 0..550: the total ice, built with
python3 tools/build_case1_total_ice.py --nc /path/to/fort.92_85_MISI.nc \
    --grounded /path/to/grounded_bin --out /path/to/case1
# -> /path/to/case1/total/icemodel/  (and totalY/, a pure resampling used as a control)

--grounded is a directory with the archived grounded-ice files of the OSF archive converted to .bin, either with the Fortran tool built next to every executable (fortran/build/case1/make_cache 512 OUTDIR FILE...) or, without a Fortran build, with Python: python python/tools/text2npy.py --dir GROUNDED_TEXT --pattern 'AISload_gd_Run85_0_0_*' --outdir OUTDIR followed by python -c "import glob, numpy as np; [np.load(f).astype('<f8').tofile(f[:-4] + '.bin') for f in glob.glob('OUTDIR/*.npy')]" (the .bin payload equals the .npy payload). Despite the _gd_ prefix, the files in total/icemodel/ hold the total ice. * earthmodel/prem_512.l60K2C.sum18p6.dum19p2.tz19p4.lm22: the Love-number file distributed with Han et al. (2022), included unchanged in lovenum/. examples/case1_forward.sh copies it there if it is missing. * grid/GLlat_512.txt, grid/GLlon_512.txt (written by tools/make_grid.py if missing). * others/topo0_archive (text; optionally converted with python3 python/tools/text2npy.py /path/to/INPUT_FILES/others/topo0_archive).

Run

INPUT=/path/to/INPUT_FILES bash examples/case1_forward.sh fortran
INPUT=/path/to/INPUT_FILES bash examples/case1_forward.sh python

The Fortran branch is equivalent to

CASE=case1 bash fortran/build.sh
mkdir -p RUN_case1/OUTPUT_SLM RUN_case1/ICELOAD_SLM
ln -sfn /path/to/INPUT_FILES RUN_case1/INPUT_FILES
cp fortran/build/case1/exe RUN_case1/ && cd RUN_case1
OMP_NUM_THREADS=8 OMP_STACKSIZE=32M SLEVOLVE_INNER=extrap \
SLEVOLVE_SNAP=550 SLEVOLVE_SNAP_FIELDS=tgrid ./exe 550

and the Python branch to

python3 python/run_ais.py --steps 550 --threads 8 --sht ducc --lmax 511 --opt all --inner extrap \
    --icedir /path/to/INPUT_FILES/icemodel \
    --topo /path/to/INPUT_FILES/others/topo0_archive \
    --earth /path/to/INPUT_FILES/earthmodel/prem_512.l60K2C.sum18p6.dum19p2.tz19p4.lm22 \
    --save-fields tgrid,ocean --out OUT_case1_py

Check either output against the shipped reference:

python tests/check_reference.py --case case1 --dir OUT_case1_py              # Python
python tests/check_reference.py --case case1 --dir RUN_case1/OUTPUT_SLM      # Fortran

The Fortran example writes only tgrid0 and tgrid550, so for it check_reference.py compares dtopo_550 and the inner-iteration counts (from the text file OUTPUT_SLM/numiter), reports the other reference fields as SKIP and lists them at the end. For the Fortran example output it reported dtopo_550 max |diff| 8.2e-12 m and identical iteration counts (2099). To compare all fields, run the Fortran example with SLEVOLVE_SNAP=1,100,550 SLEVOLVE_SNAP_FIELDS=tgrid,ocean.

Expected result. Topography change at step 550 (reference/case1/dtopo_550.npy, south polar stereographic view and global Mollweide view; colormap PuOr_r with fixed limits +-400 m as in Fig. 3a of the paper, arrows on the colour bar for values beyond; maximum 390 m; black line: coast of the initial topography):

The unloading of the West Antarctic ice sheet raises the bed by up to 390 m after 550 years on this low-viscosity Earth, with subsidence where ice thickens. Area-weighted RMS 12.3 m; 2099 inner iterations in 550 steps.

Variants

  • Legacy-equivalent run (exact, comparable to the legacy solver): the same with SLEVOLVE_INNER=off (Python: --inner off).
  • All snapshots: omit SLEVOLVE_SNAP (or set SLEVOLVE_SNAP=all).

docs.title: Case 2: two glacial cycles (1200 × 0.2 kyr), one pass
docs.text:
Data (about 640 MB): OSF, Han et al. (2022), doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/8PTFM: Data/SeaLevelModel_TwoGlacialCycle_Simulations/INPUT_NHIS2GC.zip (630 MB; iceload0 .. iceload1200) and Data/CoupledModel_OneGlacialCycle_Simulations/INPUT_Others/etopo2_512_ice6gC (8.4 MB). The Love numbers are shipped (lovenum/prem_512.l120C.ump5.lm5).

Input tree

bash tools/prepare_case2_inputs.sh ICEDIR TOPO EARTH GRIDDIR /path/to/INPUT_FILES
  • ICEDIR: iceload0..iceload1200 extracted unchanged from INPUT_NHIS2GC.zip (OSF archive).
  • TOPO: etopo2_512_ice6gC (OSF archive).
  • EARTH: the Love-number file for the Case 2 Earth model, lovenum/prem_512.l120C.ump5.lm5 (the archived file is corrupt; see Benchmark provenance). The case2 preset compiles in this PLANETMODEL name; rebuild with PLANETMODEL=<your file name> to use another file.
  • GRIDDIR: directory with GLlat_512.txt and GLlon_512.txt (written by tools/make_grid.py if they are missing).
  • The script needs make_cache: build first with fortran/build.sh (e.g. CASE=case2), or set MAKE_CACHE.

Settings (CASE=case2): L_sim = 240000, dt1..4 = 200, norder = 511, initial_topo = .false., topomodel = etopo2_512_ice6gC, driver run_outer_plus.

Run (first outer pass from the present topography):

INPUT=/path/to/INPUT_FILES bash examples/case2_one_pass.sh fortran
INPUT=/path/to/INPUT_FILES bash examples/case2_one_pass.sh python

The Fortran branch builds with CASE=case2, sets up RUN_case2/ and runs OMP_NUM_THREADS=8 OMP_STACKSIZE=32M SLEVOLVE_INNER=extrap ./exe 1200 1. The Python branch runs

python3 python/run_outer.py --iters 1 --inner extrap --opt all --lmax 511 --threads 8 \
    --inputs /path/to/INPUT_FILES --icepfx iceload --nfiles 1201 --dt 200 \
    --topo-pres /path/to/INPUT_FILES/others/etopo2_512_ice6gC \
    --earth /path/to/INPUT_FILES/earthmodel/prem_512.l120C.ump5.lm5 --save-steps 1,600,1200 --out OUT_case2_py
python tests/check_reference.py --case case2 --dir OUT_case2_py

The paper reports this case as one pass only.

Expected result. Topography change at step 1200 of the pass from the present topography (reference/case2/dtopo_1200.npy, Mollweide view; colormap PuOr_r with fixed limits +-200 m, the 99th percentile of |change| (173 m) rounded up, arrows on the colour bar for values beyond; maximum 283 m; black line: present coast):

The largest changes are under the former North American and Eurasian ice sheets. Area-weighted RMS 27.4 m, which is also the outer misfit of this pass (reference/case2.json, misfit_rms).

docs.title: Case 3: ICE-NADI-1 (50 × 0.5 kyr), full outer iteration
docs.text:
Data: Zenodo, Lucas et al. (2026), doi:10.5281/zenodo.21464139: ICE-NADI-1.nc; and from the OSF archive of Case 2 the present topography etopo2_512_ice6gC (8.4 MB). The Love numbers are shipped (lovenum/prem_512.l96C.ump3.lm1).

Input tree

python3 tools/prepare_case3_nadi.py --out /path/to/INPUT_FILES --ice-nc /path/to/ICE-NADI-1.nc \
    --grid /path/to/grid --topo /path/to/etopo2_512_ice6gC   # --grid optional (make_grid.py)
mkdir -p /path/to/INPUT_FILES/earthmodel
cp lovenum/prem_512.l96C.ump3.lm1 /path/to/INPUT_FILES/earthmodel/

This writes icemodel/nadi_0..50, others/topo_pres, grid/. Store the ICE-NADI-1 ice as <f8: it is not f4-lossless (File formats §4).

Run

INPUT=/path/to/INPUT_FILES bash examples/case3_ice_age.sh fortran 5   # 5 outer passes
INPUT=/path/to/INPUT_FILES bash examples/case3_ice_age.sh python 5

The script first builds the segmented, partially relaxed initial topography (skipped if T0_segmented.npy exists in the current directory):

python3 python/init_topo_segmented.py --inputs /path/to/INPUT_FILES --icepfx nadi_ --nfiles 51 \
    --dt 500 --earth /path/to/INPUT_FILES/earthmodel/prem_512.l96C.ump3.lm1 --lmax 511 \
    --out T0_segmented.npy

--dt is the step length in years (500), as for run_outer.py; the script converts it to kyr internally and prints both. The fixed point starts from the present topography unless --start is given; a .json file with the segments is written next to the output.

Fortran (in-process outer driver): the script builds with CASE=case3 and calls

OMP_NUM_THREADS=8 OMP_STACKSIZE=32M SLEVOLVE_INNER=extrap SLEVOLVE_REUSE=warm INPUT=/path/to/INPUT_FILES \
  bash examples/run_outer_mem.sh case3 case3 5 T0_segmented.npy

examples/run_outer_mem.sh RUNNAME BUILDTAG NOUTER TOPO0 [LAST=50] runs fortran/build/BUILDTAG/exe in ./runs/RUNNAME. With TOPO0=pres it runs passes 1..NOUTER from the present topography. Otherwise it seeds tgrid0_1 = TOPO0 (.npy, <f8) and pred_pres_topo_1 = the present topography, then runs passes 2..NOUTER+1 in one process (./exe LAST K0 K1). The present topography is TOPO_PRES=<path> (default INPUT/others/topo_pres, the Case 3 file): a .npy file (or <path>.npy when it exists) is read directly, any other file as grid text with the build's text2npy (grid NLAT x NLON, default 512 x 1024). The wrapper needs no Python (bash, od, awk). The log is run_mem.log.

Python:

python3 python/run_outer.py --iters 5 --inner extrap --reuse warm --lmax 511 --threads 8 \
    --inputs /path/to/INPUT_FILES --earth /path/to/INPUT_FILES/earthmodel/prem_512.l96C.ump3.lm1 \
    --topo0 T0_segmented.npy --out OUT_case3_py

Check the result:

python tests/check_reference.py --case case3 --dir OUT_case3_py --topo-pres /path/to/INPUT_FILES/others/topo_pres

Expected result. Topography change at step 50 of pass 5 (reference/case3/dtopo_p5_s50.npy, Mollweide view; colormap PuOr_r with fixed limits +-600 m, the 99th percentile of |change| (512 m) rounded up, arrows on the colour bar for values beyond; maximum 1025 m; black line: present coast):

From 25 ka to the present the topography rises by up to about 1 km under the former North American and Fennoscandian ice and falls by about 100 m over the oceans, the deglacial rise of sea level relative to the sea floor.

The outer misfit, the area-weighted RMS of predicted minus observed present topography, falls from 12.0 m after pass 1 to 0.074 m after pass 5 (reference/case3.json, misfit_rms).

The figures of this page are made with python tools/plot_reference.py --outdir DIR --topo1 T1 --topo2 T2 --topo3 T3 from reference/, where T1, T2, T3 are the topographies whose 0 m contour is drawn as the coast (Case 1: INPUT_FILES/others/topo0_archive; Case 2: etopo2_512_ice6gC; Case 3: topo_pres); how the runs correspond to the paper is in Reproducing the published results.

docs.title: File conversion
docs.text:
This page lists the converters between the legacy text format, .npy, the legacy .bin cache and NetCDF, in Fortran and Python.

task Fortran (fortran/tools/; built by fortran/build.sh into fortran/build/<case>/ (e.g. fortran/build/case1/), or by fortran/tools/build_npytools.sh into fortran/tools/bin/) Python (python/tools/) text -> npy text2npy [--f4] [--nlat N --nlon M] [--outdir D] FILE... or --dir D --prefix P --range K0 K1 text2npy.py [--f4] [--nlat N] [--nlon M] [--outdir D] FILE... or --dir D --pattern 'P*' npy -> text npy2text [--format F] [--ncol 1024] [--outdir D] FILE.npy... npy2text.py [--format F] [--ncol N] [--outdir D] FILE... text -> LE f8 .bin (legacy cache) make_cache NGLV OUTDIR FILE [FILE...] none npy snapshots -> NetCDF4 none npy2nc.py RUNDIR --out run.nc [--fields tgrid,ocean] [--times F / --dt Y] [--earth E] [--solver S] [--lon-convention solver\|sampled] [--attr k=v] [--zlib]

Text formats (--format):

name layout used by es16.9 (default) %16.9E (Fortran ES16.9E2), one value per line the solver's own text output (write_sl) row-e16.7 %16.7e, 1024 per line, no separator OSF archive topography / tgrid files row-e.18 %.18e, 1024 per line, ' ' separator OSF Case 1 ice files (np.savetxt default) row-E18.10 %18.10E, 1024 per line, ' ' separator Case 3 (ICE-NADI-1) ice files written by tools/prepare_case3_nadi.py

npy2nc.py coordinates: * lat = asin of the solver's Gauss-Legendre nodes (sht.gaulw, the same as GLlat_512.txt to 5e-7 deg), north to south. * lon = i*360/1024, the solver's SHT grid and GLlon_512.txt. --lon-convention sampled gives the (i+1)*360/1024 mapping, which is the mapping the archived Case 1 ice was sampled with (see tools/regrid.py). It is not the solver grid. * time comes from OUTPUT_SLM/times when present, otherwise from step*dt. * The global attributes carry the solver, the Earth model and the planet constants (solver.Planet, with run_log.json rhoi/radius overrides). For Fortran builds with LEGACY_CONSTANTS=1, pass --attr overrides.

The .npy layout is specified in File formats; the --f4 rule in File formats.

docs.title: Degree-1 Love numbers and reference frames
docs.text: This page explains the degree-1 frame of the shipped Love-number files and the degree-1 collocation initialisation defect (a copy of lovenum/DEGREE1_NOTES.md).

docs.title: 1. Degree-1 frames
docs.text:
At degree 1 a rigid translation of the Earth is a free mode, so h_1, l_1 and k_1 are defined only once an origin is chosen. Moving the origin adds the same constant to h_1, l_1 and k_1. Common conventions: - CM (centre of mass of Earth + load): k_1 = -1; - CE (centre of mass of the solid Earth): k_1 = 0; - CF (centre of surface figure): h_1 + 2 l_1 = 0.

All Love-number files in lovenum/ use the CE frame (k_1 = 0) for their elastic and fluid limits (see Sect. 2 for the degree-1 samples of the Case 1 file), and SLEvolve applies no frame conversion: degree-1 displacement and geoid outputs are in the frame of the Love-number file. Differences such as h_1 - k_1 and l_1 - k_1 do not depend on the frame, and sea level, which depends on 1 + k - h, is frame-independent.

docs.title: 2. The degree-1 collocation initialisation defect
docs.text:
The collocation method (Peltier 1985; Mitrovica and Peltier 1992) fits sum_j a_j/(s_i + s_j) = X(s_i) - X_el at fixed poles s_i, where X_el is the elastic limit (s -> infinity), computed separately. By construction the left side is the relaxation part only: it vanishes as s -> infinity. The fit therefore assumes that the samples X(s_i) and the limit X_el are in the same degree-1 frame.

In earlier library files (the Love-number library of Austermann and Mitrovica 2015, from which the Case 2 file was previously taken), the degree-1 samples were initialised in CM while the limits were in CE. In plain terms: every sample then carries a constant offset of -1 in h, l and k, and a sum of decaying terms a_j/(s + s_j) cannot represent a constant, so the fit compensates with large alternating residues; the degree-1 relaxation curves h_1(t), l_1(t) and k_1(t) are then wrong by the same time-dependent amount. The Case 2 and Case 3 files in lovenum/ were computed with the samples and limits in the same frame, which removes the defect (their degree-1 k residues are exactly 0). The Case 1 file (prem_512.l60K2C.sum18p6.dum19p2.tz19p4.lm22, distributed with Han et al. 2022 and included unchanged) carries the same degree-1 defect, with no effect on sea level and topography.

Because the same error enters h, l and k, it cancels in h - k: sea level and topography are unaffected (degree-1 h - k, a dimensionless Love number, unchanged to 3e-5). The separately output degree-1 fields (radial displacement, geoid and horizontal displacement) differ.

docs.title: File formats
docs.text:
This page specifies the binary containers of the grid and spectral files.

Both solvers use NumPy .npy as their binary format. NetCDF is only an export format, made from Python. Text in the list-directed grid format of the legacy code of Han et al. (2022) is handled by converters.

docs.title: 1. Grids (ice, topography, tgrid/ocean/beta/R/G snapshots)
docs.text:
property value container .npy version 1.0 (2.0 if the header exceeds 64 KiB), 64-byte-aligned header shape (nlat, nlon) = (512, 1024) fortran_order False dtype <f8. Ice inputs may be <f4, but only when they are lossless (see §4). Masks may be |i1 element order the stream order of the text files, i.e. a[j, i]: j = Gauss-Legendre row (north to south), i = longitude column payload identical to the legacy headerless .bin cache (numpy.fromfile(f, "<f8"))

Header written by both codes (identical):

\x93NUMPY \x01\x00 v\x00 {'descr': '<f8', 'fortran_order': False, 'shape': (512, 1024), }<spaces>\n

A <f4 ice cache has the same header with 'descr': '<f4'. The payload starts at byte 128.

In Fortran, the payload is read straight into data_slm(nglv, 2*nglv). This fills the array exactly as read(u,*) data_slm fills it from the text file. The array's storage order is the stream order (the SHT treats longitude as fastest). In numpy, np.load(f) gives a with a.ravel() == the text stream.

docs.title: 2. Spectral fields (dS_converged<N>.npy)
docs.text: <c16, shape (L+1, L+1) with L = NORDER, fortran_order=True, so that a[l, m] == dS(l, m) (zero for m > l). The payload is again identical to the legacy dS_converged<N>.bin. The Python solver writes the same thing (npyio.save_spectral) when --io-compat fortran is set (the default).

docs.title: 2.1 Optional horizontal-displacement outputs
docs.text:
• horiz<N>.npy (Fortran SLEVOLVE_HORIZ=1|2; Python run_ais.py --horizontal; run_outer.py --horizontal writes horiz<N>_it<k>.npy): the spectral scalar Psi_lm, same container and convention as dS_converged<N>.npy (<c16, (L+1, L+1), fortran_order=True, spharmt U convention, a[l, m], zero for m > l and for l = 0). Units: metres.
  • Psi<N>.npy (Fortran SLEVOLVE_HORIZ=2): Psi synthesised on the grid, grid layout of §1.
  • utheta<N>.npy, uphi<N>.npy (Python --horizontal-grid, or python/tools/horiz_grad.py horiz<N>.npy for Fortran output): grid layout of §1, <f8, metres. u_theta = dPsi/dtheta (theta = colatitude, positive southward), u_phi = (1/sin theta) dPsi/dphi (positive eastward); u_north = -u_theta.
  • In snapshot mode (SLEVOLVE_SNAP) the Fortran fields are named horiz and Psi in SLEVOLVE_SNAP_FIELDS (all includes them). Convention and verification: Horizontal displacement.

docs.title: 3. File naming and switches (Fortran)
docs.text:
• Snapshots: OUTPUT_SLM/<field><N>.npy with field in tgrid, ocean, beta, dS_converged, R, G (optional: horiz, Psi, §2.1), the names of the legacy .bin files with .npy in place of .bin. SLEVOLVE_SNAP / SLEVOLVE_SNAP_FIELDS select what is written. snap_index.txt lists step field file dtype n1 n2.
  • SLEVOLVE_FMT=npy (default) | bin selects the output container (bin = the old headerless stream).
  • Inputs: for every grid <path>, the solver tries <path>.npy, then <path>.bin, then the text file <path>. This covers ice caches, the initial topography and pred_pres_topo_/tgrid0_. The .npy files may be <f8, <f4, |i1, <i4 or <i8, in either order. f4 is promoted exactly.
  • Not converted, on purpose: the exact-memory checkpoint (exact_memory_state_<i>.bin, SLEVOLVE_CKPT, off by default) and the file-mode warm-reuse store (reuse_<i>.bin, SLEVOLVE_REUSE=warm without in-memory outer iterations). Each is a multi-array record file with its own magic, shape check and random-access record layout, and each is read only by the solver that wrote it. A single .npy cannot hold them; the .npz equivalent would need zip I/O.

The Python solver (run_ais.py, run_outer.py) writes tgrid<N>.npy, R, G in the same layout. With --io-compat fortran (the default) it writes ocean<N>.npy / beta<N>.npy as <f8 (0/1) like the Fortran code; --io-compat legacy restores uint8. It reads ice, topography and --topo0 through python/slevolve/npyio.py (.npy > .bin > text).

docs.title: 4. f4 losslessness of the ice inputs
docs.text:
• AIS grounded ice AISload_gd_Run85_0_0_{0..550}: 551/551 files exactly representable in float32. <f4 caches are lossless; a 20-step run from them gives identical output (Release notes).
  • nadi ice nadi_{0..50} (printed %18.10E from float32 values): 0/51 exact. Only 81-88 % of cells round-trip, because 11 significant digits of a float32 value do not parse back to a float32. These are stored as <f8.
  • archived Case 1 topography (8 significant digits): not exact (19 % of cells) -> <f8.

text2npy --f4 checks this per file and falls back to <f8 with a warning. It never loses data.

The converters are described in File conversion; development checks of the formats in Release notes.

docs.title: 5. Portability
docs.text:
fortran/src/npy_io_mod.f90 is self-contained: it depends only on iso_fortran_env, not on any solver module. Its minimal interface:

  • read_grid(a, path, ios[, source, errmsg]): .npy > .bin > text
  • read_ice_cache(a, path, ios, ...): same lookup
  • write_grid(a, path, ios[, dtype='f4'|'f8']): f4 is used only when lossless
  • write_snapshot(a|z, path, ios): real grid, or complex spectral field (fortran_order)

It also has a low-level layer (npy_read_header, npy_read_r8, npy_read_c16, npy_write_r8/c16/i1, npy_f4_exact). The solver-side hook is the solver I/O module in fortran/src/, which uses only read_grid, write_grid and write_snapshot.

docs.title: Horizontal displacement output
docs.text:
This page explains how to switch on, write and post-process the optional horizontal (tangential) surface displacement and states its conventions.

Applies to the Fortran solver (fortran/src/) and the Python solver (python/). The feature is off by default. Switching it on changes no other output (see Checks made during development).

docs.title: 1. Implementation
docs.text:
The horizontal displacement is read from the same recursive modal states R_k as the radial displacement (paper Eqs. 2–10). Only the weights change: l_k/s_k replaces h_k/s_k.

Psi_lm(t_n) = T_l [ l^E_l L_lm + sum_k (l_k/s_k) R_k,lm ]
            + delta_l2 [ l^T_2 Lambda_2m + sum_k (l^T_k/s_k) R^Lambda_k,m ] / g
u_h = grad_h Psi:   u_theta = dPsi/dtheta,   u_phi = (1/sin theta) dPsi/dphi
Fortran Python switch SLEVOLVE_HORIZ=0 (default) / 1 / 2 run_ais.py, run_outer.py: --horizontal, --horizontal-grid weights exact_spec%a_hl = resl/s, a_thl = tresl/s (degree 2), allocated only when the switch is on (solver module fortran/src/sl_model_mod.f90, after the spectrum build) ExactMemory.horizontal_weights (solver.py) read-out modal_state_mod::state_read_horizontal (type-bound procedure). It reads the current states and leaves them unchanged. It is called after the R synthesis and before commit. ExactMemory.read_horizontal ([k,l,m] layout), ExactMemoryFast.read_horizontal ([l,k,m]), SeaLevelSolver.horizontal_lm. These are called at the same point in solver.py and solver_opt.py step() and returned as r["horiz"]. coefficient output OUTPUT_SLM/horiz<N>.npy (<c16, (L+1,L+1), fortran_order, spharmt U convention, like dS_converged) horiz<N>.npy (run_outer.py: horiz<N>_it<k>.npy at --save-steps and the last step) grid output SLEVOLVE_HORIZ=2: Psi<N>.npy (the synthesized scalar) --horizontal-grid: utheta<N>.npy, uphi<N>.npy snapshot mode field names horiz, Psi for SLEVOLVE_SNAP_FIELDS; all includes them. They are written only when SLEVOLVE_HORIZ is set. —

Files: * python/slevolve/horiz.py: gradient(U, nlat, nlon) gives (u_theta, u_phi). It maps U to ducc0 a_lm in the same way as sht_ducc.py and runs the ducc0 spin-1 synthesis_2d(..., mode="GRAD_ONLY") on the GL grid. * python/tools/horiz_grad.py: horiz<N>.npy → utheta<N>.npy, uphi<N>.npy. This is the post-processing path for Fortran output. --selftest checks against analytic fields. * python/tools/horiz_history_check.py: verification only: checks the recursive read-out against the explicit full-history sum.

What is left to post-processing. The Fortran code does not compute the gradient. A clean d/dtheta needs either a dP_lm/dtheta table, which the on-the-fly Legendre backend does not have (getuv and cosgrad need the pnm/hnm tables, which are not allocated in the SHT=otf (default), SHT=blas and SHT=exact builds; only SHT=ref keeps them), or the recurrence sin(theta) dP_l^m/dtheta = l eps_{l+1,m} P_{l+1}^m − (l+1) eps_{l,m} P_{l-1}^m. That recurrence needs degree L+1, which the existing spec2spat (degree ≤ L) cannot synthesize. Fortran therefore writes Psi_lm (and optionally Psi on the grid), and python/tools/horiz_grad.py forms u_theta and u_phi.

docs.title: 2. Conventions (checked in code and data)
docs.text:
• Love-number file. The radial path uses elast(1,l) = h^E and resh = h_k without scaling. k is stored as l·k (ke = elast(3)/l, resk/l). The l (tangential) numbers are stored the same way, as l·l: elast(2,l) and resl. The code divides resl and tresl by l, and the elastic value as well: l^E_l = elast(2,l)/l, l^T_2 = telast(2,2)/2. Evidence from the Case 1 file prem_512.l60K2C…lm22:
  • degree 2, load: 0.0481/2 = 0.024;
  • degree 2, tidal: 0.168/2 = 0.084 (the PREM tidal l_2);
  • high degree: l·l^E → about 1.15;
  • for degrees 2, 10 and 100, elastic + Σ_k residue_k/s_k reproduces the asymptotic (fluid) line for h, l and k alike. The elastic value and the residues therefore carry the same factor.

Note: in this reader elast(3,:) is l·k (it feeds ke); the l column is elast(2,:). * Normalization. T_l = 4πa³/(M(2l+1)) is the factor of the radial R (eq. B16), so T_l L_lm is the load potential divided by g. Then u_r = h·(Φ/g) and u_h = l·∇₁(Φ/g), where ∇₁ is the dimensionless surface gradient. Psi and u are in metres. The instantaneous load term is exactly the one used for R: rhoi*deltaicestar + rhow*deltaS_prev + rhow*load_inc_lm. The rotational term uses h → l and exact_trr → the tidal-l sum over r_lambda. * Directions. theta is colatitude, so u_theta > 0 is southward (u_north = −u_theta). u_phi > 0 is eastward. Grid rows run north to south and column 0 is phi = 0. Since the elastic l_l > 0 at all degrees l >= 2 of the shipped Love-number files (degree 1 depends on the frame), the elastic motion points toward added load and away from ice loss. * Spectral convention. The spharmt U convention, as in dS_converged. The Python raw-mode backend works in V = (−1)^m U and converts before output.

docs.title: Checks made during development
docs.text:
Verification checks on short runs of Case 1 and Case 3 (Fortran: SHT=otf, FFTW, 8 threads; Python: ducc, --opt all). They were not repeated for this release.

  1. Default off changes nothing.
  2. Case 1, 20 steps (./exe 20, inner off): a build without the feature, the build with the switch unset and the build with SLEVOLVE_HORIZ=2 give identical output files (154 common files, including tgrid20, R20, G20, dS_converged20, ocean20 and numiter).
  3. Case 3, two outer passes (./exe 50 2 3, extrap + warm, from a segmented initial topography): all 75 output files identical, including pred_pres_topo_2/3, tgrid0_* and numiter*.
  4. Python: run_ais.py 20 steps with and without --horizontal --horizontal-grid gives identical tgrid20, dS_converged20 and numiter; run_outer.py one pass (Case 3) with and without --horizontal gives identical pred_pres_topo_1.
  5. Fortran vs Python Psi_lm, Case 1, 20 steps. The largest difference over all coefficients and all 20 steps, relative to max|Psi_lm|, is 8.9e-13 (--opt all); 2.2e-13 to 4.2e-12 for the base SeaLevelSolver path (steps 1 and 5). The two codes' tgrid20 differ by 9.1e-13 m. The Fortran Psi20.npy equals the ducc0 synthesis of horiz20.npy to 6.7e-16.
  6. Recursion vs explicit full-history sum (python/tools/horiz_history_check.py, Case 1, 20 steps, L = 511). The quantity Σ_k (l_k/s_k) R_k,lm(t_n) was compared with Σ_{j<n} ΔL_lm(j) Σ_k (l_k/s_k)(1 − e^{−s_k (t_n−t_j)}), built from the committed increments. The largest relative difference is 1.4e-12, below 2e-13 from step 3 on. The rotational (tidal-l) term agrees to 2.5e-14.
  7. Gradient. horiz_grad.py --selftest (64×128, L = 63, analytic Psi with m = 0, 1, 2) gives max errors of 2.8e-12 for u_theta and 3.3e-13 for u_phi.
  8. Magnitude sanity check. Case 1, 550 × 1 yr, Fortran, SLEVOLVE_INNER=extrap, SLEVOLVE_HORIZ=2, gradient from horiz_grad.py. Nothing was tuned.
  9. Maximum south of 60°S: |R| = 380.5 m (77.4°S, 252.4°E). The maximum horizontal displacement is |u_h| = 56.4 m (81.3°S, 241.5°E), where the ice thickness changed by −1136 m. The ratio of the maxima is 0.15.
  10. RMS over the cells with |R| > 10 % of max|R| (10,565 cells): u_h/R = 0.17.
  11. At the step-0 ice edge south of 60°S (3,786 cells): RMS u_h = 12.3 m and RMS R = 26.6 m, a ratio of 0.46. The median pointwise ratio is 0.79. Near the edge, R falls off faster than its gradient.

The horizontal displacement is a fraction of the radial one, largest at the margins of the unloading region.

docs.text: This page specifies the run-directory layout and the ice, topography, grid and Earth-model (Love-number) input files, their units and names.

RUN/

    icemodel/   <icemodel><k>[.npy|.bin]        k = 0..N   ice thickness, m

docs.title: Grid files
docs.text:
Grid files. GLlat_512.txt holds the 512 Gauss-Legendre latitudes in degrees, north to south, and GLlon_512.txt the 1024 longitudes i * 360/1024 in degrees east, one value per line. Neither solver reads them (Fortran passes the names but opens no grid file); they document the grid, and tools/prepare_case3_nadi.py uses them to check the ICE-NADI-1 grid. tools/make_grid.py --outdir INPUT_FILES/grid writes them; examples/case1_forward.sh, tools/prepare_case2_inputs.sh and tools/prepare_case3_nadi.py call it when the files are missing. Compared with the OSF archive files, GLlon_512.txt is identical and 58 of the 512 lines of GLlat_512.txt differ in the last printed digit (maximum 5.3e-7 degrees).

Where the file names come from

  • Fortran: the names are compiled into user_specs_mod (icemodel, planetmodel, topomodel, topo_initial, gridfolder, timearray).
  • build.sh sets gridfolder = 'INPUT_FILES/grid/' and the names from PLANETMODEL, ICEMODEL, TOPOMODEL, TOPO_INITIAL (or a CASE preset, Command-line options). Without them: icemodel='AISload_gd_Run85_0_0_', planetmodel='prem_512.l60K2C.sum18p6.dum19p2.tz19p4.lm22', topomodel = topo_initial = 'topo0_archive'.

docs.title: Grid and spectral formats (summary)
docs.text:
See File formats (also fortran/IO_FORMATS.md) for the full specification.

  • Grids.
  • Container: .npy v1.0, '<f8', shape (512, 1024), fortran_order=False.
  • Element order: the stream order of the legacy text files (row = Gauss-Legendre latitude from north, longitude fastest).
  • The payload is identical to the legacy headerless .bin.
  • Ice inputs may be <f4 only where this is lossless. text2npy --f4 checks per file and falls back to <f8.
  • Spectral. dS_converged<N>.npy: '<c16', shape (L+1, L+1), fortran_order=True, so that a[l,m] = dS(l,m).
  • Input lookup. For every grid <path> the solver tries <path>.npy, then <path>.bin, then the text file <path>. Python follows the same order (npyio.read_grid).
  • Legacy-format record files (not converted): the checkpoint exact_memory_state_<i>.bin and the file-mode warm store reuse_<i>.bin.

docs.title: Times file (optional; non-uniform time steps)
docs.text:
Without a times file every step has the same length (Fortran: the build-time DT; Python: --dt), and ice file k is the ice at time k * dt. A times file gives the time of every ice file instead, so that the steps can differ in length:

  • Format. Plain text, one number per line: t_0, t_1, ..., t_N, the time of ice file k in years, for k = 0..N (N + 1 lines, as many as ice files). Any real number format that Fortran list-directed input and numpy.loadtxt read (0, 12.5, 1.25e4). t_0 may be 0 or any other value (e.g. -26000 for 26 ka before present); the times must be strictly increasing (time runs forward from file 0, the initial state, to file N). Extra lines after t_N are ignored by Fortran; Python run_ais.py uses the first --steps + 1 values, run_outer.py and init_topo_segmented.py require exactly one value per ice file.
  • Step length. Step j (from file j-1 to file j) has length dt_j = t_j - t_(j-1). The load is constant over each step, as for uniform steps.
  • Fortran. Detected automatically at INPUT_FILES/others/times; the environment variable SLEVOLVE_TIMES=<path> selects another file and SLEVOLVE_TIMES=off ignores it (Options). With a times file, build with DT unset (it defaults to 1 and then only counts steps, NSTEPS). Without one, the build-time DT (any integer) is the uniform step. The executable prints non-uniform time steps from <file>: ... when a times file is used.
  • Python. --times FILE on run_ais.py, run_outer.py and init_topo_segmented.py (--dt is then ignored). Python does not look for the file by itself.
  • A uniform times file (t_k = t_0 + k * dt) with an integer or exactly representable dt gives the same result as the run without a times file exactly (zero difference).

docs.title: Love-number (Earth model) file
docs.text:
The file is the plain-text output of a collocation Love-number calculation (Mitrovica and Peltier 1992); degree-1 conventions are described in Degree-1 Love numbers. It is read once per run in the solver module fortran/src/sl_model_mod.f90 (block "Read in Love numbers" in sl_solver, run once via pp_love_ready), as in the legacy code:

(header line, skipped)
for each degree l = 1..norder:
  l  K_l                                   (degree, number of modes)
  s_1 .. s_K                               inverse relaxation times, 1/kyr
  h^E  l*l^E  .  .  l*k^E                  elastic load Love numbers (l and k multiplied by l)
  h^F  l*l^F  .  .  l*k^F                  fluid limit (t -> infinity), read but not used
  r_1 .. r_K        (h residues)
  l_1 .. l_K        (l residues, multiplied by l)
  r'_1 .. r'_K      (k residues, multiplied by l)
  for l >= 2: the same five lines for the tidal Love numbers (h^T, l*l^T, l*k^T, residues)
  • The l scaling was checked on the Case 1 file: degree 2 gives 0.0481/2 = 0.024 (load l'_2) and tidal 0.168/2 = 0.084 (PREM tidal l_2), and for every degree and all three numbers elastic + sum_k residue_k/s_k reproduces the asymptotic (fluid-limit) line, so elastic values and residues carry the same factor l.
  • The code divides the k and l values by l, and sets he = h^E, ke = k^E/l, r = h residues, rprime = k residues, rT, rprimeT (tidal), as in Kendall et al. (2005).
  • Units: the state decay factor is exp(-s * dt_years / 1000) (modal_state_mod::update_decay), so s is in 1/kyr. The recursion uses the residue weights (r'-r)/s, r/s and, for degree 2, the rotational terms r'/s, r'_T/s, (r'_T-r_T)/s.
  • Only degrees 1..norder are read; the file may contain more.
  • modal_state_mod::spectrum_load reads a different, pre-reduced spectrum file (LMAX MAXMODES, then per mode s and six weights). The solver does not call it; the spectrum is built in memory from the Love-number file.
  • Python reads the same Love-number file with solver.LoveNumbers.

How to write a file for your own Earth model: Love numbers.

docs.title: Get the code
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/xiyuanbao/slevolve && cd slevolve

All commands in this manual are run from this directory (the release root).

docs.title: Fortran
docs.text:
Toolchain. gfortran, FFTW 3, OpenMP and (outside macOS) OpenBLAS, all from conda-forge:

conda create -n slevolve-fortran -c conda-forge gfortran fftw openblas llvm-openmp
conda activate slevolve-fortran

This environment was created and used to build and pass the Fortran test on the tested machine. On macOS the build links Apple Accelerate for BLAS; elsewhere it links the OpenBLAS of the environment (BLASLIB=openblas, the default on Linux; not tested). Instead of activating the environment you can pass CONDA_ENV=slevolve-fortran to the build script.

Build.

CASE=case1 bash fortran/build.sh

takes about 10 s and ends with the line

built: /path/to/slevolve/fortran/build/case1/exe (case=case1 driver=run_from_zero_plus sht=otf ...)

The tools make_cache, text2npy and npy2text are built into the same directory. The linker may print ld: warning: duplicate -rpath ... ignored (once per linked program); this is harmless. Running ./exe without arguments prints the arguments the driver expects, e.g. usage: ./exe LAST (driver run_from_zero_plus: forward run of steps 1..LAST; the step length is the build-time DT). To check the build, run the Fortran test (Verifying the installation).

Build directory. fortran/build/<CASE>/ for CASE=case1|case2|case3, fortran/build/custom/ without CASE. A switch that differs from its default adds a suffix (SHT=blas gives case1_blas, OMP=0 gives case1_serial, NSTEPS=20 gives case1_N20); TAG=<name> sets the name directly.

Positional arguments fortran/build.sh [TPW] [CHECKMARINE] [NSTEPS]. Normally none is given.

argument values default meaning TPW T, F T rotational feedback (true polar wander) CHECKMARINE T, F T marine check: ice that would float on the current topography is removed from the load NSTEPS integer from CASE (550 without CASE) number of time steps compiled in (L_sim = DT * NSTEPS); also settable as NSTEPS=

Switches and when to choose them (environment variables; full table in Command-line options):

switch default when to change it CASE=case1\|case2\|case3 unset to build one of the benchmark cases: sets the file names, DT, NSTEPS, INITIAL_TOPO and the driver of that case. Unset for your own case, with the file names given explicitly (Setting up a new case) DRIVER from CASE; run_from_zero_plus run_from_zero_plus: forward run, ./exe LAST, step length DT. run_outer_plus: one outer pass per process, ./exe LAST [ITERSL]. run_outer_mem: several outer passes in one process, ./exe LAST K0 K1 (fastest for ice age runs) DT from CASE; 1 step length in integer years; must equal the time spacing of your ice files. The forward driver uses the build-time DT (any integer); non-uniform steps come from a times file (Input files) INITIAL_TOPO from CASE; T T: forward run from a known initial topography (TOPO_INITIAL); F: ice age run, outer iteration on the initial topography from the present topography TOPOMODEL PLANETMODEL, ICEMODEL, TOPOMODEL, TOPO_INITIAL from CASE; Case 1 names your file names in INPUT_FILES/earthmodel/, icemodel/ (prefix), others/ NORDER 511 maximum degree. 511 is the largest degree resolved by the 512 Gauss latitudes and is used by all benchmark cases; 512 (the legacy default) remains selectable SHT otf Legendre transform. otf (on-the-fly recurrence) is the fastest from about 4 threads up and needs half the memory of blas; blas (precomputed table and DGEMM) can be faster on 1-2 threads. exact and ref are for verification only (they reproduce the legacy transform) OMP 8 any value other than 0 compiles with OpenMP; the number of threads is set at run time with OMP_NUM_THREADS. OMP=0 builds a serial executable FFT fftw fft991 uses the FFT routine of the legacy code (no FFTW needed; slower) SYM 1 north-south symmetry in the transform (faster; same result to round-off). SYM=0 for checks only BLASLIB accelerate on macOS, else openblas the BLAS library (OPENBLAS_PREFIX if not in the conda env) EPS1 1.0E-5 inner-iteration tolerance epsilon1 LEGACY_CONSTANTS=1 unset ice density 910 kg m^-3 and radius 6.371229e6 m of the older legacy code, instead of 920 and 6.371e6 (Han et al. 2022) FC, FFTW_PREFIX, OPENBLAS_PREFIX, CONDA_ENV gfortran, $CONDA_PREFIX toolchain without an activated conda env (not tested)

Compiler flags: -O3 -ffree-line-length-none -fdefault-real-8 -fdefault-double-8 -cpp.

Build all three benchmark cases

CASE=case1 bash fortran/build.sh    # -> fortran/build/case1/exe   forward run, ./exe 550
CASE=case2 bash fortran/build.sh    # -> fortran/build/case2/exe   one outer pass per process, ./exe 1200 1
CASE=case3 bash fortran/build.sh    # -> fortran/build/case3/exe   in-process outer iteration, ./exe 50 K0 K1

docs.title: Fortran without Python
docs.text:
The Fortran solver, its tools and the Fortran-only test need no Python. The ice age wrapper examples/run_outer_mem.sh needs no Python either. The segmented first-pass initial topography (python/init_topo_segmented.py) and the input-preparation scripts in tools/ do; without Python, start the outer iteration from the present topography (TOPO0=pres) or supply your own .npy. Instead of conda, the toolchain can come from the system package manager. Only the macOS/conda route above was tested here; the commands below are given for convenience and have not been run on this release.

macOS (Homebrew):

brew install gcc fftw openblas libomp
FC=gfortran-15 FFTW_PREFIX=$(brew --prefix fftw) \
  NSTEPS=8 ICEMODEL=synth_ice_ TOPOMODEL=synth_topo PLANETMODEL=prem_512.l96C.ump3.lm1 \
  bash fortran/build.sh

Homebrew installs gfortran with its major version in the name (gfortran-15 or similar; check ls $(brew --prefix)/bin/gfortran*). On macOS the build links Apple Accelerate for BLAS; to use the Homebrew OpenBLAS instead add BLASLIB=openblas OPENBLAS_PREFIX=$(brew --prefix openblas). gfortran brings its own OpenMP runtime (libgomp); libomp is only needed if you build with clang-based tools.

Debian/Ubuntu (apt):

sudo apt install gfortran libfftw3-dev libopenblas-dev
FC=gfortran FFTW_PREFIX=/usr BLASLIB=openblas OPENBLAS_PREFIX=/usr \
  NSTEPS=8 ICEMODEL=synth_ice_ TOPOMODEL=synth_topo PLANETMODEL=prem_512.l96C.ump3.lm1 \
  bash fortran/build.sh

build.sh links -L$FFTW_PREFIX/lib -lfftw3 and -L$OPENBLAS_PREFIX/lib -lopenblas. On Debian/Ubuntu the libraries are in /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu (or /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu), which the linker searches by default, so /usr works even though /usr/lib itself does not hold them.

variable meaning Homebrew apt FC Fortran compiler gfortran-15 (versioned name) gfortran FFTW_PREFIX prefix of lib/libfftw3 $(brew --prefix fftw) /usr BLASLIB accelerate or openblas accelerate (default on macOS) openblas (default elsewhere) OPENBLAS_PREFIX prefix of lib/libopenblas (with BLASLIB=openblas) $(brew --prefix openblas) /usr

Then run the Fortran-only test with the same variables in the environment:

FC=... FFTW_PREFIX=... bash tests/test_fortran_synthetic.sh

It builds the solver, generates the synthetic Earth with the Fortran generator tools/make_synthetic_case.f90 (same Earth and files as the Python generator), runs 8 steps and compares the result with the shipped reference reference/synthetic/tgrid8.npy.

docs.text:
• Python 3 with numpy, numba, ducc0 and scipy (for the --sht numpy backend). Optional: netCDF4 for python/tools/npy2nc.py and the input-preparation scripts. Tested versions under Tested environment.
  • Two routes, same code and options: run the scripts in python/ directly (no install step), or install the package slevolve with pip (Python: pip install) and use the console scripts.
  • run_ais.py and run_outer.py pin thread counts before NumPy is imported.

Environment:

conda create -n slevolve -c conda-forge python=3.12 numpy numba ducc0 scipy netcdf4 matplotlib
conda activate slevolve

Check it with python tests/run_all.py (Verifying the installation).

docs.title: Python: pip install
docs.text:
The Python solver is also the package slevolve (sources in python/slevolve/, metadata in pyproject.toml at the release root). From a clone:

pip install .                 # numpy, scipy
pip install '.[fast]'         # plus numba and ducc0 (needed for --opt numba, --sht ducc, run_outer, init-topo)
pip install -e '.[all]'       # editable install for development; all = fast + plot (matplotlib) + netcdf (netCDF4)

Extras: fast (numba, ducc0), plot (matplotlib), netcdf (netCDF4), all. Python >= 3.10.

Console scripts (same options as the scripts; --help lists them):

console script script in the repository slevolve-forward python/run_ais.py slevolve-outer python/run_outer.py slevolve-init-topo python/init_topo_segmented.py slevolve-text2npy python/tools/text2npy.py slevolve-npy2text python/tools/npy2text.py slevolve-npy2nc python/tools/npy2nc.py

For example the Case 1 forward run of Benchmarks becomes slevolve-forward --steps 550 --sht ducc --opt all --inner extrap --lmax 511 --icedir ... --topo ... --earth lovenum/... --out .... In Python: import slevolve (slevolve.__version__, slevolve.SeaLevelSolver, slevolve.OptSeaLevelSolver, slevolve.LoveNumbers, slevolve.Planet, slevolve.SHT, slevolve.make_sht; loaded on first use, so import slevolve does not import NumPy).

The wheel contains only the Python package. The Fortran solver, the Love-number files (lovenum/), the tests, the examples, the input-preparation tools (tools/) and the reference data (reference/) are in the repository, not in the wheel; pass the Love-number file with --earth. Ice caches built by slevolve-forward without --icedir and by slevolve-outer go to python/cache/ in a checkout (also for an editable install), else to ~/.cache/slevolve; SLEVOLVE_CACHE_DIR overrides both.

docs.title: Lineage and references
docs.text:
This page describes the code lineage of SLEvolve and lists the references of that lineage.

The pseudo-spectral solution of the sea-level equation was developed by Mitrovica and Peltier (1991) and extended to a rotating Earth by Milne and Mitrovica (1998); its numerical formulation with migrating shorelines and the outer iteration on the initial topography is that of Kendall et al. (2005), which SLEvolve retains in full. Only the evaluation of the viscous history term is changed.

The ice age sea-level code implementing this formulation was written at Harvard by S. Goldberg (2015-2016, senior thesis supervised by J. X. Mitrovica; see also Goldberg et al., 2016), as recorded in the headers of his source and of the released legacy code. It was modified by E. N.-H. Chan (McGill University, 2017-2019) for text input and output and a Mars option, and then extended by Han et al. (2022) into 1DSeaLevelModel_FWTW with the forward algorithm of Gomez et al. (2010), an ice-sheet coupling interface following Gomez et al. (2012) and the time window algorithm (MIT license). The Fortran version of SLEvolve is derived from that code; the Python version was written from scratch following the same formulation. SLcode (Austermann and Mitrovica, 2015) is an independent implementation of the same formulation.

docs.title: Love numbers
docs.text:
This page explains how to supply Love numbers for your own Earth model and how to write them with python/tools/write_lovenum.py.

SLEvolve reads precomputed Love numbers; it does not compute them. For another Earth model, compute the load and tidal Love numbers in normal-mode form (elastic part, fluid limit, and per mode an inverse relaxation time and residues for h, l and k) with an external normal-mode or collocation code (for example your own), and write them with python/tools/write_lovenum.py. The three shipped files are the only tested inputs:

file lithosphere upper mantle viscosity lower mantle viscosity used in prem_512.l60K2C.sum18p6.dum19p2.tz19p4.lm22 60 km 10^18.6 Pa s (60-200 km), 10^19.2 Pa s (200-400 km), 10^19.4 Pa s (400-670 km) 10^22 Pa s (from the file name; see Benchmark provenance) Case 1 (Han et al. 2022 file, unchanged) prem_512.l120C.ump5.lm5 120 km 5e20 Pa s 5e21 Pa s Case 2 (collocation) prem_512.l96C.ump3.lm1 96 km 3e20 Pa s 1e21 Pa s Case 3, the quick start and the Fortran test (collocation)

All three use the PREM elastic and density structure and hold degrees 1-512. The file names encode the structure: l<km> lithosphere thickness, ump<x> upper mantle viscosity x 10^20 Pa s, lm<x> lower mantle viscosity x 10^21 Pa s (lm22 in the Case 1 name: 10^22 Pa s).

Layout read by both solvers (solver.LoveNumbers; Fortran block "Read in Love numbers"). Each group starts on a new line and may continue over several lines (Fortran list-directed reads):

line(s) content 1 header, free text, skipped per degree l = 1, 2, ..., L (consecutive, from 1; no degree 0) a l K_l: degree and number of modes; K_l may differ between degrees, at most 500 b s_1 .. s_K: inverse relaxation times, 1/kyr, positive c h^E l*l^E x x l*k^E: elastic loading Love numbers; the two middle values are read and ignored (0 in the shipped files) d h^F l*l^F x x l*k^F: fluid limit, same layout; read, not used e, f, g K_l residues each, 1/kyr: h; l multiplied by l; k multiplied by l only for l >= 2: h to l the same five groups (c to g) for the tidal Love numbers
  • h is stored as is; l and k (elastic, fluid and residues) are multiplied by the degree l, and the readers divide by l.
  • The response to a unit load applied at t = 0 is h(t) = h^E + sum_k (r_k / s_k) (1 - exp(-s_k t)) with t in kyr (the code uses exp(-s_k dt / 1000) with dt in years); the same for l and k.
  • The solver reads the first lmax degree blocks; the file may hold more.
  • Degree 1 must be in the frame you want for the degree-1 outputs: SLEvolve applies no frame conversion. The shipped files are in the CE frame, k^E_1 = 0 (Degree-1 Love numbers and reference frames).
  • The tidal numbers enter only with rotation on (tpw), at degree 2.

write_lovenum.py provides write_lovenum(path, header, hE, lE, kE, hF, lF, kF, s, rh, rl, rk, ...) (arrays per degree, unscaled; the docstring has a complete example) and write_from_lovenumbers(path, love, header). The command line form rewrites a file through the reader:

python python/tools/write_lovenum.py --from lovenum/prem_512.l96C.ump3.lm1 --lmax 512 --out copy.txt

For all three shipped files this reproduces every number of the original to a relative 4.2e-16 (maximum absolute difference 1.1e-13).

The line-by-line read of the file by the solvers is specified in Input files. Degree-1 frames and the collocation initialisation defect of the Case 1 file are discussed in Degree-1 Love numbers and reference frames.

docs.title: Method overview
docs.text: This page summarises the formulation, the recursive modal state and its placement rule, the changes to the iteration starts, and where each change is in the code, and lists the core equations of the paper with every symbol explained.

docs.title: Formulation
docs.text:
SLEvolve solves the gravitationally self-consistent sea-level equation on a spherically symmetric (1-D) viscoelastic Earth. It uses the normal-mode (Love-number) formulation of Kendall et al. (2005) as implemented in the legacy code of Han et al. (2022), called the legacy solver in this guide.

The legacy solver evaluates the viscous response at every time step as an explicit sum over the whole load history. The cost per step therefore grows with the step number, and the total cost grows as O(N^2). SLEvolve replaces that sum with a recursive normal-mode state: one state per mode, degree and order, advanced by one decay factor per step. The cost per step is then independent of the length of the history, and the total cost is O(N). The recursion is exact. It covers all six history terms of the legacy solver: sea level, radial displacement, and the four degree-2 rotational terms.

There are two implementations.

  • Fortran (fortran/src/). Derived from the legacy code.
  • Python (python/). Written from scratch following the same formulation, built on NumPy, Numba and ducc0.

What is exact and what is not.

  • These parts are exact and reproduce the legacy solution to round-off (< 1e-11 m in final topography, identical inner-iteration counts and masks):
  • the recursive state,
  • resident I/O,
  • the transform reductions,
  • the Legendre and FFT backends,
  • OpenMP.
  • These parts change only the starting point of an iteration, never the equations:
  • the extrapolated inner start,
  • the warm start across outer passes,
  • the partially relaxed initial topography.

The converged result of each step then agrees with the legacy result within the inner tolerance epsilon1, not exactly.

docs.title: Core equations
docs.text: The equations below are those of the paper (Sect. 2), in its notation: \(\Delta\) denotes a change since the first time \(t_0\), \(\delta\) an increment over one step. Equation numbers are those of the paper.

docs.title: Sea-level equation (Eq. (1) of the paper)
docs.text:
\[ \Delta S_j = \Delta\mathcal{SL}_j\,C_j\beta_j - T_0\,(C_j\beta_j-C_0\beta_0),\qquad \Delta\mathcal{SL}_j=\Delta\mathcal{G}_j-\Delta\mathcal{R}_j+\frac{\Delta\Phi_j}{g} \]
  • \(t_0<t_1<\dots<t_N\): the time steps; \(\delta t_j=t_j-t_{j-1}\) the step length (may be non-uniform).
  • \(\Delta S_j\): change of ocean height since \(t_0\) (the ocean load, as water thickness) at step \(j\).
  • \(\Delta\mathcal{SL}_j\): change of sea level (sea surface minus solid surface) since \(t_0\).
  • \(\Delta\mathcal{G}_j\): geographically variable part of the change of the sea-surface equipotential (geoid change).
  • \(\Delta\mathcal{R}_j\): change of the radial position of the solid surface (radial displacement).
  • \(\Delta\Phi_j/g\): the uniform term, a spatially constant shift of the sea surface fixed by conservation of ice-plus-ocean mass; \(g\) is the surface gravity.
  • \(C_j\): ocean function, 1 where sea level is positive (sea surface above the solid surface), 0 elsewhere.
  • \(\beta_j\): ice function, 0 where grounded ice covers the surface, 1 elsewhere. The marine check: marine ice counts as grounded only where its thickness exceeds the water depth times \(\rho_w/\rho_I\); thinner ice floats and is not part of the load.
  • \(T_0\): topography at \(t_0\); prescribed in a forward run, found by the outer iteration in an ice age run.

The equation is nonlinear because \(C_j\) and \(\beta_j\) depend on the sea level being solved for. At each step an inner (Picard) iteration on the ocean-load increment \(\delta S_j\) runs until its relative change between iterates falls below \(\epsilon_1\) (default \(10^{-5}\)).

docs.title: Response to the load (Eqs. (2)-(5) of the paper)
docs.text:
For each spherical-harmonic coefficient \((\ell,m)\):

\[ \Delta\mathcal{SL}_{\ell m}(t_j)=T_\ell\left[E_\ell\,\Delta L_{\ell m}(t_j)+V_{\ell m}(t_j)\right],\qquad T_\ell=\frac{4\pi a^3}{M_e(2\ell+1)},\qquad E_\ell=1+k^E_\ell-h^E_\ell \]
  • \(a\), \(M_e\): radius and mass of the Earth.
  • \(\Delta L_{\ell m}(t_j)=\sum_{n=0}^{j}\delta L^n_{\ell m}\): cumulative load change; \(\delta L^n_{\ell m}=\rho_I\,\delta I^{*\,n}_{\ell m}+\rho_w\,\delta S^n_{\ell m}\) the load increment of step \(n\), with \(\delta I^{*}\) the increment of grounded ice thickness (marine ice included where grounded) and \(\rho_I\), \(\rho_w\) the ice and water densities.
  • \(E_\ell\): elastic sea-level response, from the elastic load Love numbers \(h^E_\ell\) (radial) and \(k^E_\ell\) (potential).
  • \(V_{\ell m}\): viscous (hereditary) response. At degree 2 the rotational feedback adds \(g^{-1}[E^T_2\,\Delta\Lambda_{2m}+V^T_{2m}]\), with the tidal Love numbers and the centrifugal potential perturbation \(\Lambda\), formed in the same way.

The viscoelastic Love numbers are finite sums of decaying exponentials (Eq. (4)):

\[ h_\ell(t)=h^E_\ell\,\delta(t)+\sum_{k=1}^{K_\ell} r^\ell_k\,e^{-s^\ell_k t},\qquad k_\ell(t)=k^E_\ell\,\delta(t)+\sum_{k=1}^{K_\ell} r^{\ell\prime}_k\,e^{-s^\ell_k t} \]
  • \(K_\ell\): number of modes at degree \(\ell\) (16 to 26 in the benchmark Earth models).
  • \(s^\ell_k>0\): inverse relaxation time of mode \(k\); \(r^\ell_k\), \(r^{\ell\prime}_k\): its residues (modal amplitudes) for radial displacement and potential; \(\delta(t)\): Dirac delta.

A load increment persists after it is applied, so its viscous response is the time integral of the impulse response, \((r/s)(1-e^{-st})\) per mode: the response to a step load increment is the elastic term plus a sum over modes of \(a_k(1-e^{-s_k t})\). The full-history form of the viscous term is (Eq. (5))

\[ V_{\ell m}(t_j)=\sum_{n=0}^{j-1}\beta_\ell(t_j-t_n)\,\delta L^n_{\ell m},\qquad \beta_\ell(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{K_\ell} a^\ell_k\left(1-e^{-s^\ell_k t}\right),\qquad a^\ell_k=\frac{r^{\ell\prime}_k-r^\ell_k}{s^\ell_k} \]
  • \(\beta_\ell(t)\): viscous step-response kernel of the sea level (not the ice function \(\beta_j\)).
  • \(a^\ell_k\): modal weight of mode \(k\) for sea level. The radial displacement uses the weights \(r^\ell_k/s^\ell_k\) of the same modes. This sum costs \(O(j)\) at step \(j\), \(O(N^2)\) in all; it is what the legacy solver evaluates (six such sums: sea level, radial displacement and four degree-2 rotational terms).

docs.title: Recursive modal state (Eqs. (8) and (10) of the paper)
docs.text:
\[ V_{\ell m}(t_j)=\sum_{k=1}^{K_\ell}a^\ell_k\,R^k_{\ell m}(t_j),\qquad R^k_{\ell m}(t_j)=d^\ell_k(\delta t_j)\,R^k_{\ell m}(t_{j-1})+\bigl(1-d^\ell_k(\delta t_j)\bigr)\,\Delta L_{\ell m}(t_{j-1}),\qquad d^\ell_k(\delta t_j)=e^{-s^\ell_k\,\delta t_j} \]
  • \(R^k_{\ell m}(t_j)\): the modal state of mode \(k\), one field per mode, degree and order; \(R^k_{\ell m}(t_0)=0\). It is defined as \(\Delta L_{\ell m}(t_{j-1})-Q^k_{\ell m}(t_j)\) with \(Q^k_{\ell m}(t_j)=\sum_{n=0}^{j-1}e^{-s^\ell_k(t_j-t_n)}\delta L^n_{\ell m}\) (Eq. (7)).
  • \(d^\ell_k(\delta t_j)\): one-step decay factor of mode \(k\) over the step length \(\delta t_j\); a non-uniform step changes only \(d\).
  • The update is algebraically identical to the full-history sum for any sequence of increments; it costs one multiply-add per mode and coefficient per step, \(O(N)\) in all. The rotational terms carry their own states with the same update.

docs.title: Placement rule (Sect. 2.4 of the paper)
docs.text:
An increment applied at \(t_j\) has zero viscous age at \(t_j\) (\(\beta_\ell(0)=0\)), so \(V_{\ell m}(t_j)\) depends only on the converged \(\Delta L(t_{j-1})\). Hence:

  1. advance-and-read: before the inner iteration of step \(j\), the states are advanced once with the update above and \(V_{\ell m}(t_j)\) is read from them; it stays fixed during the iteration;
  2. the inner iteration updates only the elastic and uniform terms, \(C_j\), \(\beta_j\) and \(\delta S_j\);
  3. commit: after convergence, \(\Delta L_{\ell m}(t_j)=\Delta L_{\ell m}(t_{j-1})+\delta L^j_{\ell m}\).

Trial iterates never enter the stored history, so every iteration sees exactly the viscous response of the full-history sum, and both formulations take the same inner iterations.

docs.title: Extrapolated inner start (Sect. 2.5 of the paper)
docs.text:
\[ \delta S^{(0)}_j=\delta t_j\left[\dot S_{j-1}+\left(\dot S_{j-1}-\dot S_{j-2}\right)\frac{\delta t_j+\delta t_{j-1}}{\delta t_{j-1}+\delta t_{j-2}}\right],\qquad \dot S_i=\frac{\delta S_i}{\delta t_i} \]
  • \(\delta S^{(0)}_j\): first guess of the ocean-load increment of step \(j\) (superscript 0: initial iterate).
  • \(\dot S_i\): rate of the converged increment of step \(i\).
  • For uniform steps this is \(2\,\delta S_{j-1}-\delta S_{j-2}\). The first two steps use the eustatic guess (the mass of the ice increment spread uniformly over the ocean), which the legacy solver uses at every step. Only the starting point changes; the converged result agrees within \(\epsilon_1\).

docs.title: Outer iteration and partially relaxed initial topography (Eqs. (11) and (12) of the paper)
docs.text:
\[ T_0\leftarrow T_0-\left(T_{\mathrm{pred}}-T_{\mathrm{obs}}\right) \]
  • \(T_{\mathrm{pred}}\): present topography predicted by a pass (a full forward run); \(T_{\mathrm{obs}}\): observed present topography. The misfit is the area-weighted RMS of \(T_{\mathrm{pred}}-T_{\mathrm{obs}}\).

First-pass initial topography from the partially relaxed response:

\[ T_0=T_{\mathrm{obs}}+\sum_i\mathcal{SL}^{\mathrm{seg}}_i,\qquad h^{\tau_i}_\ell=h^E_\ell+\sum_k\frac{r^\ell_k}{s^\ell_k}\left(1-e^{-s^\ell_k\tau_i}\right) \]
  • \(i\): monotonic segments of the global ice-volume history (split at its extrema; changes below 1 % of the volume range ignored). The superscript seg marks a quantity of one whole segment (neither a one-step increment δ nor a change since \(t_0\), Δ).
  • \(I^{\mathrm{seg}}_i\): net change of grounded ice over segment \(i\); \(\tau_i\): its mean age at the end of the run, weighted by the ice-volume change of each step.
  • \(h^{\tau_i}_\ell\), \(k^{\tau_i}_\ell\) (the latter with \(r^{\ell\prime}_k\)): Love numbers partially relaxed to age \(\tau_i\).
  • \(\mathcal{SL}^{\mathrm{seg}}_i\): sea-level response to \(I^{\mathrm{seg}}_i\) with these Love numbers; the sea-level equation is solved once for the summed response, with the water load evaluated with the segment-averaged Love numbers \(h^w_\ell=\sum_i w_i h^{\tau_i}_\ell\), \(w_i=|V^{\mathrm{seg}}_i|/\sum_j|V^{\mathrm{seg}}_j|\) (\(V^{\mathrm{seg}}_i\): net ice-volume change of segment \(i\)). Implemented in python/init_topo_segmented.py.

docs.title: What changed relative to the legacy code
docs.text:
Section numbers refer to Sect. 2 of the paper.

# Change Where (Fortran / Python) Arithmetic changed? 1 Recursive modal state. Two calls per step: advance-and-read before the inner iteration (decays the state by one step and returns the viscous sums), commit after convergence (adds the converged load increment). This placement rule keeps the recursion identical to the full-history sum inside the nonlinear iteration. fortran/src/modal_state_mod.f90, module modal_state_mod: state_init, update_decay, state_advance_and_read, state_commit, state_save_checkpoint / state_load_checkpoint. Python: kernels.py::advance_and_read, commit_add; solver_opt.py::ExactMemoryFast Exact (reformulation of the same sum; round-off level) 2 Resident state and binary I/O. One process runs all steps. Earth model, modal state, step-0 fields and transform tables stay in memory. Grids are read and written as binary (.npy, see Input files). solver I/O module in fortran/src/ (pp_read_grid, pp_write_grid, pp_write_cplx), npy_io_mod.f90 (read_grid, read_ice_cache, write_grid, write_snapshot); driver run_from_zero_plus.f90. Python: npyio.py (read_grid, save_grid, save_spectral, IceDir) No. SLEVOLVE_COMPAT restores the legacy re-reads (diagnostic) 3 Fewer transforms per step, 5n+6 → 3n+2 (n = inner iterations), grouped into 2n+1 Legendre sweeps. opt_read_options, flags diag, dsl, lazyrg, icebatch, rt, merge (SLEVOLVE_OPT). Python: --opt raw,diag,dsl,numba,sums (solver_opt.py::parse_opts) Order of operations only. SLEVOLVE_OPT=none switches the reductions off 4a Legendre backend: table. Precomputed P_lm applied as a BLAS matrix product (DGEMM), with N–S symmetry. fortran/src/spharmt_otf.f90: spharm_blas_ana, spharm_blas_syn, sht_sym; build SHT=blas Order of operations only 4b Legendre backend: on-the-fly recurrence. No table; recurrence in m, vectorized over latitude, OpenMP over m. Used for the benchmark runs in the paper. spharmt_otf.f90 + otf_kernels.inc; build SHT=otf Order of operations only 5 FFTW in place of FFT99. docs.title: Horizontal (tangential) displacement: convention
docs.text:
For a spherically symmetric Earth the surface horizontal displacement is the surface gradient of a scalar, read out from the same modal states R_k as the radial displacement with different weights:

Psi_lm(t_n) = T_l [ l^E_l L_lm(t_n) + sum_k (l_k / s_k) R_k,lm(t_n) ]          (l >= 1, metres)
            + delta_l2 [ l^T_2 Lambda_2m(t_n) + sum_k (l^T_k / s_k) R^Lambda_k,m(t_n) ] / g
u_theta = dPsi/dtheta ,   u_phi = (1 / sin theta) dPsi/dphi
  • T_l = 4 pi a^3 / (M (2l+1)) (eq. B16, the factor of the radial R), L_lm the total surface load (ice + ocean, kg m^-2) in the same instantaneous form as R (rhoi*deltaicestar + rhow*deltaS_prev + rhow*load_inc_lm), Lambda the rotational driving potential (same terms as the R rotation with h replaced by l). l^E_l = elast(2,l)/l, l_k = resl(k,l) (after the division by l), l^T_2 = telast(2,2)/2, l^T_k = tresl(k,2). So T_l L_lm is the load potential divided by g, and u_r = h (Phi/g) and u_h = l grad_1 (Phi/g) (grad_1 = dimensionless surface gradient).
  • theta is colatitude, so u_theta > 0 points south; u_north = -u_theta; u_phi > 0 points east. Grid rows run north to south and column 0 is phi = 0 (the solver grid).
  • With l > 0 the elastic horizontal motion points toward a positive load (away from a region of ice loss).
  • Coefficients are written in the spharmt (U) convention of dS_converged (both codes; Python converts from its raw-mode V convention).
  • Fortran: SLEVOLVE_HORIZ (0 default). The weights a_hl = l_k/s_k, a_thl are added to the spectrum only when the switch is on; modal_state_mod::state_read_horizontal reads the current states between advance-and-read and commit and does not change them. With 0 (or with any value) every other output is identical to the build without the feature.
  • The grid gradient is not computed in Fortran (the on-the-fly Legendre backend has no dP/dtheta table); it is formed from horiz<N>.npy by python/tools/horiz_grad.py (ducc0 spin-1 gradient synthesis, python/slevolve/horiz.py), which is also what Python --horizontal-grid uses.
  • Usage: Horizontal displacement output; checks: Horizontal displacement output.

docs.title: Output fields
docs.text: This page defines every output file of the two solvers: what it holds, its sign convention, units, reference time and frame. All statements are taken from the code that writes the files (python/slevolve/solver.py, python/run_ais.py, python/run_outer.py, and the output section of sl_solver / sl_solver_init in fortran/src/sl_model_mod.f90). The binary containers are specified in File formats.

docs.title: 1. Conventions common to all fields
docs.text:
Grid layout. Every grid file is a (512, 1024) array a[j, i]. Row j is the Gauss-Legendre latitude GLlat[j], running from north (+89.73 deg) to south; column i is longitude i * 360/1024 degrees east (0 to 359.65). Longitude varies fastest in memory. tools/make_grid.py writes the latitudes and longitudes as text (Input files).

Step index. File index N is the step number. Ice file <icemodel>N is the ice thickness at the end of step N, i.e. at time N * dt after the start (with a times file: at time t_N, line N + 1 of the file; Input files); ice file 0 is the initial state. The step numbers in the output names are the same with and without a times file.

  • N = 0: the initial state, written before the first step (tgrid0, ocean0, beta0, and in Fortran dS_converged0 = 0 and TPW0 = 0).
  • N = 1: the state after the first step (time dt, or t_1 with a times file), computed with ice file 1.
  • N = k: the state after step k (time k * dt, or t_k).

Reference time. tgrid, ocean and beta are absolute (the state at the end of step N). The changes R, G and dS_converged are cumulative since step 0 (the start of the run, or of the outer pass), not increments of one step.

Sign of topography and sea level. The main variable is the topography T: the elevation of the solid surface (bedrock, without the ice) relative to the sea surface, in metres, positive up. The ocean is where T < 0. The solver updates it as T_N = T_0 - dSL_N, where dSL_N is the sea-level change since step 0 (positive = sea-level rise). So the relative sea-level change since step 0 is -(tgrid<N> - tgrid0).

Degree-1 frame. R and G contain degree 1 in the frame of the Love-number file; SLEvolve applies no frame conversion. The shipped Love-number files are in the CE frame (k_1 = 0). The Case 1 file is CE in its elastic and fluid limits but carries a degree-1 initialisation defect in its residues, which changes degree-1 R and G but not sea level or topography (lovenum/DEGREE1_NOTES.md).

Masks. ocean and beta are 0/1 fields, stored as <f8 (Python --io-compat legacy: uint8).

docs.title: 2. Grid and spectral fields (per step N)
docs.text:
file meaning units sign / reference tgrid<N> topography T at the end of step N: solid surface (bedrock) minus sea surface. tgrid0 is the initial topography of the run (or of the outer pass) m positive up (land), negative in the ocean; absolute ocean<N> ocean function C: 1 where tgrid<N> < 0, else 0. It does not look at the ice: marine cells under grounded ice have C = 1. The ocean that carries water load is C * beta 0/1 absolute beta<N> ice-free mask: 1 where the ice thickness of ice file N is zero (below machine epsilon), else 0. The raw ice file is used, before the marine check 0/1 absolute R<N> radial displacement of the solid surface since step 0, including the rotational term m positive up; cumulative since step 0; degree 1 in the Love-number frame G<N> change of the sea surface (geoid plus the spatially uniform term from mass conservation) since step 0, G = dSL + R m positive up; cumulative since step 0; degree 1 in the Love-number frame dS_converged<N> spherical-harmonic coefficients of the change of ocean (water) thickness since step 0, after the inner iteration of step N has converged. The water load is rhow * dS m of water cumulative since step 0 horiz<N>, Psi<N>, utheta<N>, uphi<N> optional horizontal displacement, see Horizontal displacement m since step 0

The sea-level change itself, dSL = G - R, is not written as a separate file; it equals tgrid0 - tgrid<N>.

Spectral convention of dS_converged (and horiz). Complex (L+1, L+1) array a[l, m], 0 <= m <= l, zero above the diagonal, in the convention of the legacy spharmt module (python/slevolve/sht.py): a[0, 0] is the global mean of the field (to a relative 1.7e-9, from the truncated 1.41421356 literal of the legacy source), and the field is f = sum_l [ a[l,0] c_l0(mu) + 2 Re sum_{m>=1} a[l,m] c_lm(mu) exp(i m phi) ] with c_lm = 1.41421356 * P~_lm, P~_lm orthonormal on [-1, 1] without the Condon-Shortley phase. python/slevolve/sht.py (SHT.synthesis) and sht_ducc.py synthesise it.

docs.title: 3. Scalar outputs
docs.text:
quantity meaning units Fortran file Python ocean area area of C (ocean<N> = 1) m^2 ocean_area run_log.json scalars[N].ocean_area ice-free ocean area area of C * beta m^2 oceanBeta_area scalars[N].oceanBeta_area GMSL change over the ocean area-weighted mean of the sea-level change since step 0 over C (gmslc_ocn) m (rise positive) gmslc_ocnArea scalars[N].gmslc_ocn GMSL change over the ice-free ocean the same mean over C * beta (gmslc_ocnBeta) m gmslc_ocnBetaArea scalars[N].gmslc_ocnBeta ice volume integral of the ice thickness used as load (after the marine check when it is on, i.e. grounded ice only) m^3 of ice ice_volume scalars[N].ice_volume inner iterations iterations of the ocean-load update to reach epsilon1 at each step count numiter (one line per step 1..N) numiter.npy time k * dt since the start; with a times file t_k as given in it yr times (0, dt, 2 dt, ..., one line per step 0..N, ES14.4E2; with a times file t_0, t_1, ..., t_N in ES24.16E3) not written; run_log.json has dt_years, and with --times times_years (t_0..t_N); outer_log.json has times_years rotation see below TPW<N> not written

The Fortran scalar files are text, one value per line (ES14.4E2), line 1 = step 0, line N+1 = step N (the GMSL files start with 0 at step 0). They are appended at every step and are written also in snapshot mode (SLEVOLVE_SNAP). Python stores the same quantities in run_log.json under scalars: entry 0 is step 0 (areas and ice volume only), entry N is step N. nmelt (Fortran) is the number of earlier load steps taken into account at each step, and elapsed_wall_time, elapsed_cpu_time are timings.

TPW<N> (Fortran, rotation on): three records of the converged rotational quantities after step N (TPW0 = zeros), printed in Fortran column-major order:

  1. 9 values: il(3,3), the perturbation of the inertia tensor (only il(1:3,3) is filled), kg m^2;
  2. 3 values: mm(1:3), the perturbation of the rotation vector, dimensionless (m1, m2 polar motion in radians, m3 relative change of the spin rate);
  3. 18 values: lambda(3,3), the degree-0 and degree-2 coefficients of the rotational driving potential, as (real, imaginary) pairs, m^2 s^-2.

All three are totals since step 0.

docs.title: 4. Outer iteration (ice age runs)
docs.text:
file meaning tgrid0_<p> initial topography T0 used in outer pass p (m) pred_pres_topo_<p> topography at the last step of pass p, the predicted present topography (m) tgrid<k>_it<p>.npy Python run_outer.py: topography at step k of pass p, for the steps in --save-steps T0_next.npy Python: the initial topography for the next pass (Picard: tgrid0_<p> + (T_obs - pred_pres_topo_<p>); --outer secant uses the secant update) outer_log.json Python: per pass the misfit rms_pred_minus_obs (area-weighted RMS of pred_pres_topo_<p> - T_obs, m), max_abs, the inner iterations per step and the wall time numiter_<p> Fortran run_outer_mem: copy of numiter for pass p

The Fortran files pred_pres_topo_<p>, tgrid0_<p> are written at the last step of each pass; in snapshot mode only when SLEVOLVE_OUTER is set.

docs.title: 5. Which files each driver writes
docs.text:
Fortran (OUTPUT_SLM/, .npy by default):

  • step 0: tgrid0, ocean0, beta0, dS_converged0, TPW0, and the first line of every scalar file;
  • each step N: tgrid<N>, ocean<N>, beta<N>, dS_converged<N>, R<N>, G<N>, TPW<N>, one more line in each scalar file;
  • with SLEVOLVE_SNAP=<list> only the listed steps (step 0 always) and the fields in SLEVOLVE_SNAP_FIELDS (default tgrid) are written as grids; snap_index.txt lists them. The Case 1 example (SLEVOLVE_SNAP=550 SLEVOLVE_SNAP_FIELDS=tgrid) writes tgrid0.npy and tgrid550.npy.

Python run_ais.py (--out):

  • step 0: tgrid0.npy, ocean0.npy, beta0.npy (always);
  • each step N: the fields named in --save-fields (default tgrid,ocean,beta; also R, G, dS); dS is written as dS_converged<N>.npy;
  • at the end: numiter.npy, step_wall_seconds.npy, run_log.json (settings, timings, scalars).

Python run_outer.py (--out): the files of §4, plus horiz<k>_it<p>.npy with --horizontal.

To convert: python/tools/npy2text.py (text), python/tools/npy2nc.py (NetCDF with latitude, longitude and time axes; the time comes from OUTPUT_SLM/times when present, otherwise from step * --dt; for a Python run with non-uniform steps use the times_years of run_log.json).

docs.title: 6. Files written, by solver
docs.text: Sections 1-4 define the meaning, sign, units and reference time of every output; this section is a short checklist of the files, by solver (section 5 gives the same per driver, with step detail).

docs.title: Fortran, per step N
docs.text:
• Grids tgrid<N>, ocean<N>, beta<N>, R<N>, G<N> and the spectral field dS_converged<N>. By default every field is written at every step, as .npy (SLEVOLVE_FMT=npy, SLEVOLVE_BIN=1). Text copies are written only with SLEVOLVE_TEXT=1.
  • Restrict grid output with SLEVOLVE_SNAP / SLEVOLVE_SNAP_FIELDS. OUTPUT_SLM/snap_index.txt lists what was written.
  • Scalar text files, always written and appended per step: numiter, elapsed_wall_time, TPW<N>, area, GMSL and ice-volume files.

docs.title: Fortran, at the last step
docs.text:
• pred_pres_topo_<k> and tgrid0_<k> (outer pass k).
  • These are not written in snapshot mode unless SLEVOLVE_OUTER is set.
  • run_outer_mem also copies numiter to numiter_<k> and prints == pass k wall … s.

Optional horizontal displacement (off by default; Horizontal displacement output)

  • Fortran SLEVOLVE_HORIZ=1: horiz<N>.npy (spectral Psi_lm); SLEVOLVE_HORIZ=2: also Psi<N>.npy (Psi on the grid). Python --horizontal: horiz<N>.npy; --horizontal-grid: also utheta<N>.npy, uphi<N>.npy. Grid components for Fortran output: python/tools/horiz_grad.py horiz<N>.npy.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
• tgrid<N>.npy plus the fields in --save-fields (default tgrid,ocean,beta).
  • numiter.npy and run_log.json.
  • run_outer.py writes the outer-pass files as .npy, plus the steps listed in --save-steps.
