docs.title: Setting up a new case
docs.text:
This page lists the steps from your own ice history, topography and Earth model to a run and a check of its result. The commands use the Python drivers, which need no rebuild; the Fortran equivalents are given in 6. Running. Input formats: File formats. Output fields: Output fields.

Step length

The steps must match the times of the ice files. Uniform steps: in Fortran the step is set at build time (DT=<years>, default 1; NSTEPS is the number of steps); in Python with --dt <years> on run_ais.py and run_outer.py. Non-uniform steps: a times file with the time of every ice file (format), found by Fortran at INPUT_FILES/others/times (or SLEVOLVE_TIMES=<path>) and passed to Python with --times <file>. Both solvers accept any uniform step and any non-uniform schedule.

docs.title: 1. Ice history
docs.text:
• Grid. Every ice file is a 512 x 1024 grid on the Gauss-Legendre grid of the solver: row j = latitude GLlat[j] from north to south, column i = longitude i * 360/1024 degrees east (grid files). Store it as .npy ((512, 1024), <f8), as a headerless little-endian float64 .bin, or as text in the stream order (python/tools/text2npy.py converts).
  • Units. Ice thickness in metres of ice (ice density rhoi = 920 kg m^-3, --rhoi to change).
  • Grounded or total ice. With the marine check on (--checkmarine T, the default) the solver keeps only ice that is grounded: ice of thickness H on a cell whose initial topography T0 (step 0) is not positive is kept if rhoi * H > rhow * |T0| (rhow = 1000 kg m^-3), otherwise it is treated as floating and removed from the load. You can then give the total (grounded plus floating) thickness. With the marine check off, give grounded ice only: floating ice would be counted as load.
  • File naming and time. Files <prefix>0, <prefix>1, ..., <prefix>N, one per step. File 0 is the initial state (the oldest time). With uniform spacing dt, file k is the ice at time k * dt after the start; with a times file, file k is the ice at time t_k of line k + 1 of the file (section 5). For an ice age run the last file N is the present.
  • Regridding. tools/regrid.py provides NearestSourceSampler(alat, alon, lon_shift=0, maxdist_km=...): every solver cell within maxdist_km of a source point takes the value of the nearest source point, all other cells are 0; the source grid is given by 2-D latitude and longitude arrays in degrees (any grid: lat-lon, polar stereographic, ...). lon_shift=0 samples onto the solver longitudes i * 360/1024; the default lon_shift=1 is the one-cell offset used only for the Case 1 files. Nearest-point sampling preserves thickness values but not the volume exactly, so compare the volumes. A runnable example (from the release root; numpy and scipy), with a 0.5-degree lat-lon source field made up in the script:
import sys
import numpy as np
sys.path.insert(0, "tools")                       # run from the release root
from regrid import NearestSourceSampler, gl_grid

# source: a regular 0.5-degree lat-lon grid (replace by your own arrays, e.g. read with netCDF4:
#   ds = netCDF4.Dataset("my_ice.nc"); lat1 = ds["lat"][:]; lon1 = ds["lon"][:]; H = ds["thk"][k])
lat1 = np.arange(-89.75, 90.0, 0.5)
lon1 = np.arange(0.25, 360.0, 0.5)
alon, alat = np.meshgrid(lon1, lat1)
H = np.where(alat < -65.0, 2000.0 * np.sqrt(np.clip(1 - ((alat + 90) / 25) ** 2, 0, None)), 0.0)

# nearest-source sampling onto the 512 x 1024 solver grid (lon = i * 360/1024: lon_shift=0);
# maxdist_km must exceed half the source spacing (0.5 deg ~ 56 km at the equator)
smp = NearestSourceSampler(alat, alon, lon_shift=0, maxdist_km=60.0)
Hg = smp.sample(H)
np.save("myice_0.npy", Hg.astype("<f8"))

# volume check: source cell areas on the sphere vs solver cell areas (gl_grid)
R = 6.371e6
a_src = R**2 * np.radians(0.5) * (np.sin(np.radians(alat + 0.25)) - np.sin(np.radians(alat - 0.25)))
_, _, _, _, _, area = gl_grid()
v_src, v_gl = (H * a_src).sum(), (Hg * area).sum()
print(f"ice volume: source {v_src:.4e} m^3, solver grid {v_gl:.4e} m^3, ratio {v_gl / v_src:.5f}")

It prints ice volume: source 3.1985e+16 m^3, solver grid 3.2069e+16 m^3, ratio 1.00263. Repeat the sampling for every ice file (myice_0.npy, myice_1.npy, ...).

docs.title: 2. Topography
docs.text:
• What it is. Bedrock (solid-surface) elevation relative to sea level, in metres, positive up, on the same grid. It is the elevation of the rock, not of the ice surface: the ice thickness is given separately. The ocean is where the topography is negative.
  • Regridding. A global topography on a lat-lon grid (e.g. ETOPO or GEBCO, averaged to a few arc-minutes first) is sampled onto the solver grid with the same NearestSourceSampler as the ice (a global source covers every cell when maxdist_km exceeds half the source spacing). Save it as a (512, 1024) <f8 .npy file.
  • Forward run (known initial state): the topography at the start, step 0 (run_ais.py --topo; Fortran TOPO_INITIAL).
  • Ice age run (initial state unknown): the observed present topography (run_outer.py --topo-pres; Fortran TOPOMODEL, with INITIAL_TOPO=F). The outer iteration adjusts the initial topography until the topography predicted at the last step matches it.

docs.title: 3. Love numbers
docs.text:
SLEvolve reads precomputed Love numbers; it does not compute them. Use one of the shipped files in lovenum/ or write your own Earth model's Love numbers with python/tools/write_lovenum.py; the layout is in Love numbers. The shipped files (all PREM elastic and density structure, degrees 1-512):

file lithosphere upper mantle viscosity lower mantle viscosity used in prem_512.l60K2C.sum18p6.dum19p2.tz19p4.lm22 60 km 10^18.6 Pa s (60-200 km), 10^19.2 Pa s (200-400 km), 10^19.4 Pa s (400-670 km) 10^22 Pa s (from the file name; see Benchmark provenance) Case 1 (Han et al. 2022 file, unchanged) prem_512.l120C.ump5.lm5 120 km 5e20 Pa s 5e21 Pa s Case 2 (collocation) prem_512.l96C.ump3.lm1 96 km 3e20 Pa s 1e21 Pa s Case 3, the quick start and the Fortran test (collocation)

docs.title: 4. Grid files
docs.text:
GLlat_512.txt and GLlon_512.txt list the latitudes and longitudes of the grid (degrees; latitude north to south). Neither solver reads them; they document the grid and are used by the input preparation scripts. Write them with

python tools/make_grid.py --outdir INPUT_FILES/grid

Details: Input files.

docs.title: 5. Step length and truncation
docs.text:
• Uniform dt. One fixed step length per run, equal to the spacing of the ice files. Python: run_ais.py --dt and run_outer.py --dt, both in years, and init_topo_segmented.py --dt in years. Each driver prints the step length it uses. Fortran: compiled in, build.sh DT=<years> (integer). The Fortran forward driver run_from_zero_plus uses the build-time DT (verified against Python with DT=1 and DT=5); for non-uniform steps use a times file (next item).
  • Non-uniform steps (times file). Write the time of every ice file, in years, one per line (t_0 .. t_N, strictly increasing; format). Python: --times <file> on run_ais.py, run_outer.py and init_topo_segmented.py. Fortran: put the file at INPUT_FILES/others/times (detected at start-up) or set SLEVOLVE_TIMES=<path>; build with DT unset, so that NSTEPS is the number of steps and the times file sets their lengths. Step j has length dt_j = t_j - t_(j-1), and both solvers use it in
    • the modal-state update, with decay factors d_k = exp(-s_k dt_j) recomputed at every change of step length (the recursion stays exact for the step-wise load history of the files);
    • the extrapolated inner start (--inner extrap, SLEVOLVE_INNER=extrap), which from step 3 on is dS0_j = dt_j [Sdot_(j-1) + (Sdot_(j-1) - Sdot_(j-2)) (dt_j + dt_(j-1)) / (dt_(j-1) + dt_(j-2))] with Sdot_i = dS_i / dt_i (the paper, Sect. 2.5), equal to 2 dS_(j-1) - dS_(j-2) for equal steps; steps 1 and 2 start from the eustatic guess;
    • the time stamps (Fortran OUTPUT_SLM/times holds t_0 .. t_N; Python run_log.json / outer_log.json hold times_years). A uniform times file gives the same result as the run without one exactly (zero difference).
  • dt and accuracy. The recursion is exact for the step-wise load history the files define; the load is constant between files. A shorter dt (or shorter steps where the load changes fast, with a times file) resolves the history better, and also the shoreline migration, which is updated once per step.
  • lmax. --lmax 511 on the 512 x 1024 grid, as in all benchmark cases (the ducc0 transform needs lmax <= 511 for 512 latitudes). Fortran: NORDER=511; the grid size is fixed at 512.

docs.title: 6. Running
docs.text:
Forward run (known initial topography):

python python/run_ais.py --steps N --dt DT --threads 4 --sht ducc --lmax 511 --opt all --inner extrap \
    --icedir INPUT_FILES/icemodel --icepfx <prefix> --topo INPUT_FILES/others/<topography> \
    --earth lovenum/<love file> --save-fields tgrid,ocean --out OUT

Fortran forward run. The input file names are compiled into the Fortran executable, so each new case is a build without CASE (CASE only selects the presets of the three benchmark cases; leave it unset) and with your file names:

ICEMODEL=<prefix> TOPOMODEL=<topography> PLANETMODEL=<love file> NSTEPS=N bash fortran/build.sh
# -> fortran/build/custom_N<N>/exe   (DT=1, NORDER=511, SHT=otf, OpenMP: the defaults)

Then set up a run directory: the executable reads INPUT_FILES/ and writes OUTPUT_SLM/ and ICELOAD_SLM/ (both must exist) relative to the directory it runs in.

mkdir -p RUN/OUTPUT_SLM RUN/ICELOAD_SLM
ln -s /path/to/INPUT_FILES RUN/INPUT_FILES      # icemodel/<prefix>0..N, others/<topography>, earthmodel/<love file>
cp fortran/build/custom_N<N>/exe RUN/ && cd RUN
OMP_NUM_THREADS=4 OMP_STACKSIZE=32M SLEVOLVE_INNER=extrap SLEVOLVE_SNAP=N ./exe N

SLEVOLVE_SNAP=N writes the grids of step N only (and step 0); omit it to write every step. With NSTEPS=550 the directory is custom (550 is the default). tests/test_fortran_python.sh is a complete example of this route.

Ice age run (outer iteration on the initial topography):

python python/init_topo_segmented.py --inputs INPUT_FILES --icepfx <prefix> --nfiles <N+1> --dt DT \
    --earth lovenum/<love file> --lmax 511 --topo-pres INPUT_FILES/others/<present topography> \
    --out T0_segmented.npy
python python/run_outer.py --iters 5 --inner extrap --reuse warm --lmax 511 --threads 4 \
    --inputs INPUT_FILES --icepfx <prefix> --nfiles <N+1> --dt DT \
    --topo-pres INPUT_FILES/others/<present topography> --earth lovenum/<love file> \
    --topo0 T0_segmented.npy --out OUT

run_outer.py defaults (--icepfx nadi_ --nfiles 51 --dt 500) are those of Case 3: always pass your own. Example: an ice history from 21 ka to the present every 500 yr has 43 files (<prefix>0 at 21 ka, <prefix>42 at present), so --nfiles 43 --dt 500 here, and --steps 42 --dt 500 for a forward run with run_ais.py.

Fortran: build with INITIAL_TOPO=F, DT=<years>, NSTEPS=N, your file names and DRIVER=run_outer_mem, and run the passes with examples/run_outer_mem.sh as for Case 3, with TOPO_PRES=<your present topography> (text or .npy; the default is INPUT_FILES/others/topo_pres) and your first-pass initial topography as TOPO0 (.npy; or pres to start from the present topography) (Running the benchmark cases). The Python driver prints the outer misfit rms_pred_minus_obs, the area-weighted RMS of predicted minus observed present topography (m), after each pass and records it in outer_log.json; the Fortran driver writes pred_pres_topo_<p>.npy and tgrid0_<p>.npy per pass, from which the same misfit is one numpy line (np.sqrt(np.average((pred - obs)**2, weights=gw[:, None])) with the Gauss weights gw). Run passes until it stops decreasing by a meaningful amount for your application; in Case 3 it falls from 12.0 m after pass 1 to 2.06 m after pass 2 (reference/case3.json, misfit_rms).

docs.title: 7. Checking the result
docs.text:
• python tests/run_all.py and bash tests/test_fortran_python.sh check the installation (Verifying the installation).
  • The benchmark cases and tests/check_reference.py check a full-size configuration against reference/ (Verifying the installation).
  • For your own case, look at:
  • numiter (inner iterations per step; Case 1 needs 2099 in 550 steps): compare a step that needs many more than its neighbours with the change of ocean<N> at that step;
  • the ice volume (run_log.json scalars, Fortran ice_volume) against the volume of your input files, which shows what the marine check removed;
  • the GMSL change (gmslc_ocn) against the barystatic estimate from the ice-volume change;
  • the maps tgrid<N> - tgrid0 (minus the relative sea-level change) and ocean<N> (the shoreline), e.g. python -c "import numpy as np; d = np.load('OUT/tgrid42.npy') - np.load('OUT/tgrid0.npy'); print(d.min(), d.max())"; python/tools/npy2nc.py converts the outputs to NetCDF for plotting.
  • For an ice age run: outer_log.json (misfit per pass) and tgrid0_<p>, the initial topography of the last pass.

Next: Love numbers.

docs.title: Benchmark provenance and differences from Han et al. (2022)
docs.text:
This page documents where the data of the three benchmark cases come from, the known issues of the archived files, and how the benchmark set-up differs from the archived runs of Han et al. (2022).

The input data of the three benchmark cases are not redistributed with SLEvolve. The scripts in tools/ convert the archived files into solver inputs; the commands are in the Running the benchmark cases.

docs.title: Case 1 -- Antarctic forward run (550 x 1 yr from 1950 CE)
docs.text:
Ice forcing. The extended RCP8.5, MISI-only (no cliff failure, no hydrofracturing) Antarctic ice-sheet run of DeConto et al. (2021), 1950-2500 CE, on a 10 km grid, taken from the Dryad archive of Yousefi et al. (2022), doi:10.5061/dryad.ncjsxkswm (run 85_MISI). The total (grounded plus floating) ice thickness is sampled onto the 512 x 1024 Gauss-Legendre grid with tools/build_case1_total_ice.py (sampling map in tools/regrid.py).

Earth model and topography. From the OSF archive of Han et al. (2022), doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/8PTFM, folder Data/AIS_550yr/:

  • Love-number file prem_512.l60K2C.sum18p6.dum19p2.tz19p4.lm22. This is their 'BLVZ' profile: 60-km lithosphere; viscosities 10^18.6, 10^19.2 and 10^19.4 Pa s at 60-200, 200-400 and 400-670 km depth. The file name ends in lm22 (lower mantle 10^22 Pa s), whereas DeConto et al. (2021) print 1 x 10^19 Pa s for the lower mantle (see "Differences from the runs of Han et al. (2022)" below). The file is included unchanged in lovenum/.
  • Initial (1950 CE) topography topo0_archive, taken from the archived output run.

What the OSF archive contains and what the archived run used.

  • The 551 archived ice files AISload_gd_Run85_0_0_<k> hold grounded ice only (prefix _gd_; they pass the flotation test against the archived bed with zero failures).
  • The archived output run was computed from the total (grounded plus floating) ice of the same ice-sheet run. Evidence: (i) driven by the archived grounded ice, neither the legacy code nor SLEvolve reproduces the archived topography (RMS 2.4 m at step 1 growing to 11.4 m at step 550; Antarctic RMS 28 m); (ii) the archived step 1 contains a one-off jump (ocean mean -1.52 m, far-field -1.80 m, up to +26 m along the Ronne and Ross shelf fronts) that corresponds to the removal of the floating shelves present in the initial state (total-minus-grounded volume 6.40e14 m^3) but absent from the later loads; (iii) a proxy shelf field reproduces this jump (pattern correlation 0.98).
  • The total-ice fields are not in the OSF archive and are rebuilt from the Dryad archive. The grounded part of the rebuilt ice, sampled onto the Gauss-Legendre grid, matches the archived grounded files cell by cell: correlation 0.99976-0.99981, 99.0 % of cells identical, volume ratio 1.00000-1.00005, identical maximum thickness, at every step checked (0, 1, 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, 400, 550). The remaining ~1 % of cells differ by a nearest-neighbour resampling offset at the ice margin.
  • The rebuilt files keep the prefix AISload_gd_Run85_0_0_ expected by the compiled-in file names, although they hold the total ice.

How the benchmark is run. With the total-ice forcing and the solver's own flotation check (checkmarine = .true.), which is the configuration of the archived run. Do not combine total-thickness ice with checkmarine = .false.. The archived grounded-ice loads, as distributed, can be used for an exactness comparison with the legacy code.

Legacy baseline. The legacy code of Han et al. (2022) re-reads the ice history as text at every step, in the layout and number format of the archived files. The text files are converted once to the binary format for SLEvolve; the legacy inputs are not altered.

docs.title: Case 2 -- two glacial cycles (1200 x 0.2 kyr from 240 ka)
docs.text:
Source. Same OSF archive, Data/SeaLevelModel_TwoGlacialCycle_Simulations/INPUT_NHIS2GC.zip (iceload0..1200): the Northern Hemisphere ice-sheet simulation of Han et al. (2021) repeated over two cycles, combined with ICE-6G_C for Antarctica (Argus et al. 2014; Peltier et al. 2015). Only the last 122 kyr are a realistic history; the first cycle is a repeat. Present topography etopo2_512_ice6gC from Data/CoupledModel_OneGlacialCycle_Simulations/INPUT_Others/. Input tree: tools/prepare_case2_inputs.sh.

Known issue. The Earth-model file distributed for the glacial-cycle cases, Data/CoupledModel_OneGlacialCycle_Simulations/INPUT_Others/prem_coll_512.l120C.ump5.lm5, is corrupt in the archive (1 110 755 NUL bytes in every copy; the zip CRC verifies, so it was uploaded in this state). Love numbers for the stated model (PREM elastic and density structure, 120-km lithosphere, upper mantle 5e20 Pa s, lower mantle 5e21 Pa s) are used instead. They were computed with the collocation method of Mitrovica and Peltier (1992) (after Peltier 1985) and are included in lovenum/ (prem_512.l120C.ump5.lm5). The case2 build preset uses this file name for PLANETMODEL; copy it into INPUT_FILES/earthmodel/.

docs.title: Case 3 -- ICE-NADI-1 deglaciation (50 x 0.5 kyr from 25 ka; Lucas et al. 2026)
docs.text: Source. Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.21464139. Input tree: tools/prepare_case3_nadi.py (icemodel/nadi_0..50, others/topo_pres, grid/). Earth model Earth_1 of Lucas et al. (2026) (96-km lithosphere, upper mantle 3e20 Pa s, lower mantle 1e21 Pa s). Its Love numbers were computed with the collocation method of Mitrovica and Peltier (1992) (after Peltier 1985) and are included in lovenum/ (prem_512.l96C.ump3.lm1). Copy the file into INPUT_FILES/earthmodel/.

docs.title: Grid and formats
docs.text: All cases use the 512 x 1024 Gauss-Legendre grid of Han et al. (2022), maximum degree 511. Grid files are NumPy .npy (fp64, little-endian, (nlat, nlon) in the stream order of the text files); spectral fields are .npy complex (L+1, L+1) in Fortran order. See File formats.

docs.title: Differences from the runs of Han et al. (2022)
docs.text:
Deliberate deviations of the benchmark set-up from the archived runs of Han et al. (2022), with the reason. "Not verified" marks statements that could not be confirmed from the archive or the paper.

Case 1 (Antarctic forward run).

  • Total-ice forcing instead of the archived grounded ice, with the marine check on. The 551 archived files AISload_gd_Run85_0_0_<k> hold grounded ice only, but the archived output run was computed from the total (grounded plus floating) ice (evidence above). The total ice is not in the OSF archive and is recovered from the Yousefi et al. (2022) Dryad archive of the same ice-sheet run; its grounded part matches the archived files cell by cell (correlation 0.99976-0.99981). With total ice the solver's flotation check (checkmarine = .true.) removes the floating part, as in the archived run.
  • Step-1 shelf-removal initialization not mimicked by default. The archived run let the floating shelves of the initial state enter the elastic and mass-conservation terms (and the rotational feedback) at step 1 but not the viscous memory. SLEvolve and the released legacy code include them in all terms alike, which leaves 2.05 m area-weighted RMS against the archived 550-yr topography on a 12.3 m signal (0.024 m with that initialization mimicked). The released legacy code behaves like SLEvolve, so the archived run differs from the released code in this initialization; the default follows the released code.
  • Love-number file as distributed (prem_512.l60K2C.sum18p6.dum19p2.tz19p4.lm22, unchanged). The file name says lower mantle 10^22 Pa s, whereas DeConto et al. (2021) print 1 x 10^19 Pa s for this profile. It is used as distributed because the archived run used it.
  • Initial topography topo0_archive taken from the archived output run.

Case 2 (two glacial cycles).

  • Love numbers recomputed. The archived Earth-model file prem_coll_512.l120C.ump5.lm5 is corrupt (1 110 755 NUL bytes in every copy). Love numbers for the stated model (PREM, 120-km lithosphere, upper mantle 5e20 Pa s, lower mantle 5e21 Pa s) were computed with the collocation method of Mitrovica and Peltier (1992) (lovenum/prem_512.l120C.ump5.lm5). Results therefore differ from the archived run by the difference of the Love numbers (not quantified here).
  • One pass from T_obs. Only the first outer pass (initial topography = present topography etopo2_512_ice6gC) is run, for the timing comparison; Han et al. (2022) ran the outer iteration. Number of passes in the archived run: not verified.
  • Antarctic ice from ICE-6G_C, as in Han et al. (2022) (the ice files are used as archived).

Case 3 (ICE-NADI-1). Not a case of Han et al. (2022).

  • Ice history ICE-NADI-1 (Lucas et al. 2026) with their Earth model Earth_1 (96-km lithosphere, upper mantle 3e20 Pa s, lower mantle 1e21 Pa s); Love numbers computed with the collocation method (lovenum/prem_512.l96C.ump3.lm1).
  • Present topography substituted: others/topo_pres is etopo2_512_ice6gC from the Han et al. (2022) OSF archive (tools/prepare_case3_nadi.py), not a topography distributed with ICE-NADI-1. The ICE-NADI-1 inputs used here do not include a present topography on the solver grid.
  • Ice age run with the outer iteration on the initial topography, started from the partially relaxed (segmented) guess with warm-started passes, instead of the three passes from the present topography of Kendall et al. (2005).

All cases.

  • Constants: ice density 920 kg m^-3 and Earth radius 6.371e6 m, the same as Han et al. (2022) (the default; the older legacy values 910 and 6.371229e6 are available with LEGACY_CONSTANTS=1).
  • Maximum degree 511 on the 512 x 1024 grid. The legacy code's default is norder = 512, and Han et al. (2022) describe their runs as expansions up to degree and order 512; degree 511 is the largest degree resolved by 512 Gauss latitudes (the ducc0 transform requires lmax <= nglv - 1).
  • Inner tolerance epsilon = 1e-5, the value set in the released legacy code (epsilon1 = 1.0E-5).
  • Uniform steps in each case (1 yr, 200 yr, 500 yr), with the full step-wise load history kept exactly. Han et al. (2022) also propose a time-window scheme that coarsens older loads; whether the archived runs used it: not verified.
  • Rotational feedback on (tpw = .true.) in all cases, as in the released legacy code.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This page runs a small synthetic case with the Python solver in under a second and explains what it prints and plots. The Fortran solver is checked on the same synthetic Earth at full resolution by the Fortran test.

The sea-level equation gives the change of relative sea level, the height of the sea surface (an equipotential of the gravity field) above the solid surface, caused by a change of the ice load, including the deformation of a viscoelastic Earth, the perturbation of its gravity field and rotation, and the redistribution of the meltwater over an ocean whose shoreline moves. SLEvolve solves it step by step in time, with an inner iteration at every step on the ocean-load increment until the ocean load, the deformation and the gravity field are mutually consistent.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
From the release root, in the Python environment of Installation (numpy is enough; matplotlib for the figures; no ducc0, numba or benchmark data needed):

python examples/quickstart.py

The synthetic Earth (tools/make_synthetic_case.py, here on a 128 x 256 Gauss grid; the Fortran tests use the same Earth on 512 x 1024, and tools/make_synthetic_case.f90 writes identical files in Fortran). An Earth-like random planet, the same in every run:

  • topography: a Gaussian random field on the sphere, synthesised from random spherical-harmonic coefficients (fixed seed 20261013) for degrees 2 to 200 with a power-law spectrum (power per degree proportional to l^-2), plus two broad bumps that put land at the south pole and around 60 N 130 E. A hypsometric transfer maps the field's area quantiles to Earth-like elevations: 29 % land (+5 m at the coast, a few hundred metres inland, a tail to about 2.4 km), a continental shelf at -100 to -200 m over 3 % of the area, a continental slope, and an ocean floor mostly at -3700 to -4500 m (down to about -4800 m) with mid-ocean-ridge-like rises to about -2500 m. A second random field adds low-amplitude fractal detail. The result has continents of varied size with irregular coasts, archipelagos and shelves (top left of the figure below). The field is built once in Python with the shipped spherical-harmonic transform and shipped as reference/synthetic/topography_seed.npy (512 x 1024, whole millimetres), which both generators read, so the Python and Fortran generators write identical files; on other grids it is sampled at the nearest grid point;
  • ice: two Vialov (equilibrium) profiles H = H0 (1 - (r / R)^(4/3))^(3/8), r the angular distance from the centre: a polar ice sheet on the south polar continent (centre at the pole, R = 17 degrees, H0 = 3000 m) and a mid-latitude ice sheet on the northern continent (centre 56 N 132 E, R = 12 degrees, H0 = 2500 m), both only where the initial topography is above -500 m (on land or shelf). The radii are chosen so that the ice lies on the land masses; a few cells at the margins are on the shelf, below sea level. Both melt to zero over 8 steps at fixed radius (the profile is scaled by the thickness at the centre), about 76 m of mean sea-level rise over the ocean in all:
step 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 polar ice sheet at the pole (m) 3000 2625 2250 1875 1500 1125 750 375 0 mid-latitude ice sheet at its centre (m) 2500 2400 2150 1800 1350 900 500 200 0

The quick start uses steps of 1 kyr so that the viscous response shows; maximum degree 63; Earth model lovenum/prem_512.l96C.ump3.lm1; rotational feedback and the marine (flotation) check on. The script also runs the same case with the marine check off for comparison. --topography FILE of make_synthetic_case.py replaces the synthetic topography by a real bedrock grid ((N, 2N) .npy); it is not used here.

All maps on this page are drawn with python/tools/plot_fields.py: a global Mollweide view (longitude -180 to 180) and a south polar stereographic view (0 E at the top); the black line on every map is the coast of the initial topography (its 0 m contour). Changes are drawn with the diverging colormap PuOr_r of the paper's topography-change panels, with symmetric limits fixed per figure (here the 99th percentile of |change| rounded up to a nice number) and arrows on the colour bar for values beyond the limits.

Top left: initial topography. Top right: ice thickness at step 0 (the mid-latitude sheet is in the upper right, on the northern continent). Bottom left: the polar ice sheet at step 0 in the south polar view (circles 10 degrees apart). Bottom right: the melt schedule. At step 8 both ice sheets are gone.

docs.text:
quickstart: synthetic Earth, grid 128x256, lmax 63, 8 steps of 1000 yr, rotation on, marine check on
step 1: ice  2625 m (pole)  2400 m (mid-lat)  inner iterations 6  ocean-mean RSL change  +7.990 m  far field  +8.570 m
...
step 8: ice     0 m (pole)     0 m (mid-lat)  inner iterations 7  ocean-mean RSL change +76.462 m  far field +78.062 m
inner iterations per step: [6, 4, 6, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7] (marine check off: [6, 4, 6, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7])
final RSL change, near field (82S 270E, under the polar ice):  -481.299 m (marine check off  -481.286 m)
final RSL change, intermediate (55S 0E, ocean):   +65.457 m (marine check off   +65.425 m)
final RSL change, far field (10N 180E, ocean):   +78.062 m (marine check off   +78.068 m)
quickstart: 0.1 s
figures written to . (colour limits: topography change +-600 m, ocean sea-level change +-100 m, departure from the ocean mean +-40 m; ocean mean +76.462 m)

Each step line gives the ice thickness of both sheets, the number of inner iterations needed to reach the tolerance at that step (epsilon1 = 1e-5, a dimensionless ratio of the change of the summed ocean-load coefficients between iterations; Glossary), the mean relative sea-level (RSL) change over the initial ocean (the cells with topography below zero at step 0, the same cells at every step) and the RSL change at the far-field site. The last lines give the iteration counts of both runs and the final RSL change at the three sites. RSL change is minus the change of topography. With matplotlib installed, the script writes the four figures of this page to the current directory (--outdir to change, --no-plot to skip).

docs.title: Topography at the final step
docs.text: After 8 kyr the unloaded polar continent has risen by up to about 570 m (brown = uplift), and the northern continent under the former mid-latitude ice sheet by up to about 450 m; the ocean floor has moved down relative to the sea surface by the global sea-level rise (light purple, about -76 m on average). Colour limits +-600 m (99th percentile of |change| rounded up).

docs.title: Sea-level change at the final step
docs.text:
(a) Relative sea-level change after 8 kyr over the initial ocean (land white), colour limits +-100 m. (b) The same minus its ocean-area-weighted mean of +76 m (+76.462 m): the departure from the ocean mean, colour limits +-40 m. (c) Topography change everywhere (uplift positive), colour limits +-600 m. Limits: 99th percentile of |field| over the plotted cells rounded up to a nice number; arrows on the colour bars mark values beyond them. Black: initial coast; dashed: ice margin at step 0; magenta circles: the three sites of the time series.

The meltwater raises sea level over the ocean by +76 m on average, but not uniformly. Near field: where the ice was, relative sea level falls, by 481 m at the near-field site, because the solid Earth rebounds once the load is removed (up to about 570 m of uplift in panel c) and the sea surface drops as the gravitational pull of the lost ice weakens; in the ocean next to the former ice sheets the rise is well below the mean (dark purple in panel b). Far field: away from both ice sheets sea level rises above the ocean mean, +78 m at the far-field site, about 2 m above the mean (light orange in panel b). Panel (b), the departure from the ocean mean, shows this departure from the uniform rise directly; in panel (a) the 45-82 m spread of the ocean values is a small part of the scale.

docs.title: Time series at three sites
docs.text:
Near field (left, 82 S 270 E, 8 degrees from the pole under the polar ice sheet): RSL falls throughout, by 481 m in 8 kyr, as the bed rebounds and the sea surface drops. Intermediate (55 S 0 E, ocean about 18 degrees beyond the margin of the polar ice): RSL rises by 65 m, less than in the far field, because the geoid falls near the shrinking ice. Far field (right, 10 N 180 E, open ocean far from both ice sheets): the largest rise, 78 m, slightly above the ocean mean (76 m), the far-field amplification of meltwater sea level. The dotted line in each panel is the ocean-mean change at 8 kyr (+76 m): the near-field curve ends far below it, the intermediate one below (65 m) and the far-field one above (78 m).

Effect of the marine check (dashed lines: marine check off). With the check on, ice whose thickness is less than that needed to stay grounded on a bed below sea level (rhoi * H <= rhow * |T|) is treated as floating and removed from the load. Here almost all the ice rests on land above sea level, so the check concerns only a few margin cells on the shelf: the two runs differ by less than 0.04 m at the three sites and need the same inner iterations.

docs.title: Release notes and known limitations
docs.text: This page lists the contents of v1.0, its differences from the legacy code and its known limitations.

docs.title: v1.0
docs.text:
Contents of the release

  • fortran/: the Fortran solver (src/), the build script build.sh with presets for the three benchmark cases, and the tools make_cache, text2npy and npy2text (tools/).
  • python/: the Python solver (run_ais.py forward run, run_outer.py ice age run with outer iteration, init_topo_segmented.py first-pass initial topography) and the converters and post-processing tools in python/tools/.
  • pyproject.toml: the Python solver as the pip-installable package slevolve 1.0.0 (sources in python/slevolve/, subpackage slevolve.tools; extras fast, plot, netcdf, all) with the console scripts slevolve-forward, slevolve-outer, slevolve-init-topo, slevolve-text2npy, slevolve-npy2text, slevolve-npy2nc. The scripts in python/ remain the no-install route.
  • tools/: input preparation for the benchmark cases (build_case1_total_ice.py, regrid.py, prepare_case2_inputs.sh, prepare_case3_nadi.py). No input data are redistributed.
  • lovenum/: the Love-number files of the three cases, in the degree-1 frame CE (k_1 = 0), and DEGREE1_NOTES.md on degree-1 Love numbers. Case 1 (prem_512.l60K2C.sum18p6.dum19p2.tz19p4.lm22) is the file distributed with Han et al. (2022), included unchanged; it is CE in its elastic and fluid limits but carries a degree-1 initialisation defect in its residues, which changes the degree-1 R, G and horizontal outputs but not sea level or topography. Cases 2 and 3 (prem_512.l120C.ump5.lm5, prem_512.l96C.ump3.lm1) were computed with the collocation method of Mitrovica and Peltier (1992) (after Peltier 1985).
  • tools/make_grid.py (grid files GLlat_512.txt, GLlon_512.txt) and python/tools/write_lovenum.py (Love numbers of your own Earth model in the solver's layout).
  • reference/: reference outputs of the three cases, checked with tests/check_reference.py.
  • tests/: the Python tests python tests/run_all.py (recursion vs explicit history sum, transform round trip, idealised small case, the extrapolated inner start for uniform and non-uniform steps, the small case with non-uniform steps), the Fortran test tests/test_fortran_python.sh (Fortran vs Python on a synthetic Earth), its non-uniform-step twin tests/test_fortran_python_vardt.sh (times file; also checks that a uniform times file reproduces the run without one exactly), the Fortran-only test tests/test_fortran_synthetic.sh (no Python; against reference/synthetic/tgrid8.npy) and tests/check_reference.py.
  • tools/make_synthetic_case.py and its Fortran twin tools/make_synthetic_case.f90 (synthetic-Earth input tree: an Earth-like random topography from a fixed seed, shipped as reference/synthetic/topography_seed.npy, and two melting Vialov ice sheets), python/tools/plot_fields.py (Mollweide and south polar stereographic maps with coastlines) and tools/plot_reference.py (maps of the reference results).
  • examples/: the quick start quickstart.py, run scripts for the three benchmark cases (case1_forward.sh, case2_one_pass.sh, case3_ice_age.sh, each for Fortran or Python) and the in-process outer-iteration wrapper run_outer_mem.sh.
  • docs/: this manual.

Differences from the legacy code of Han et al. (2022)

  • The viscous history terms (sea level, radial displacement and the four degree-2 rotational terms) are carried in a recursive normal-mode state, advanced by one decay factor per step, instead of an explicit sum over the load history. The recursion is exact.
  • One process runs all time steps with the Earth model, modal state and transform tables resident; binary .npy input and output, with text <-> .npy converters in Fortran and Python.
  • Fewer spherical-harmonic transforms per step; Legendre transform by an on-the-fly recurrence or a BLAS table; FFTW; north-south symmetry; OpenMP.
  • Optional extrapolated start of the inner iteration and warm start of outer passes (these change only the starting point of an iteration; the converged result agrees within the inner tolerance).
  • Ice age runs: partially relaxed (segmented) first-pass initial topography, and an in-process outer-iteration driver.
  • Optional output of the horizontal surface displacement.
  • The longitude FFT routine fft99b of the transform module is used in a corrected form.

The code lineage is described in Lineage and references.

Known limitations

  • Ice-sheet coupling. The ice-sheet coupling interface inherited from the legacy code (the coupling flag and the coupled ice-input path in fortran/src/sl_model_mod.f90) is retained in the Fortran source but is not used by any benchmark case, is absent from the Python version, and has not been tested with the recursive state in v1.0.
  • Time steps. Uniform steps (the benchmark cases use 1 yr, 200 yr and 500 yr): Python --dt in years (run_ais.py, default 1; run_outer.py; init_topo_segmented.py), printed at start-up; Fortran compiled in by build.sh DT=<years> (the forward driver run_from_zero_plus uses the build-time DT, verified against Python with DT=1 and DT=5). Non-uniform steps: an optional times file, one time in years per ice file (format), read by Fortran at run time from INPUT_FILES/others/times or SLEVOLVE_TIMES=<path> (build with DT unset) and by Python with --times <file>. The benchmark cases use uniform steps; the non-uniform mode is verified on the idealised small case and the synthetic Earth (tests/test_small_case_vardt.py, tests/test_fortran_python_vardt.sh), not on a benchmark case.

What the times file changes (step j has length dt_j = t_j - t_(j-1)):

1. the decay factors of the modal-state update, `d_k = exp(-s_k dt_j)`, recomputed whenever the
   step length changes (cached otherwise), in both solvers; the recursion remains exact for the
   step-wise load history (`tests/test_recursion.py`, `tests/test_small_case_vardt.py`);
2. the extrapolated inner start: from step 3 on,
   `dS0_j = dt_j [Sdot_(j-1) + (Sdot_(j-1) - Sdot_(j-2)) (dt_j + dt_(j-1)) / (dt_(j-1) + dt_(j-2))]`,
   `Sdot_i = dS_i / dt_i`, which is exactly `2 dS_(j-1) - dS_(j-2)` for equal steps
   (`tests/test_extrap_formula.py`);
3. the time stamps: Fortran `OUTPUT_SLM/times` holds `t_0 .. t_N` (written as `ES24.16E3` instead of
   the uniform-step `ES14.4E2`, so that non-integer times are kept); Python `run_log.json` and
   `outer_log.json` store `times_years` (`run_log.json` `dt_years` = `"variable"`);
4. Python `init_topo_segmented.py --times`: the segment ages are `t_N - t_n` instead of `dt (N - n)`.

Unchanged: the step indexing (ice file k is read at step k; the Fortran NSTEPS, L_sim/dt1, the time window TIMEWINDOW, the checkpoint cadence and the --save-steps/SLEVOLVE_SNAP step numbers count steps, not years). Without a times file the code paths are those of uniform steps, and a uniform times file reproduces them exactly. The legacy input_times/timearray flag of user_specs_mod is not used (it still stops the exact-memory path when set). * Fortran grid and names. nglv is fixed at 512, and the input file names are compiled in: every new case needs a rebuild. * Love numbers are read, not computed (Love numbers). * Python defaults. run_ais.py has development defaults for --earth, --icedir, --topo and --out, and run_outer.py the Case 3 defaults --icepfx nadi_ --nfiles 51 --dt 500; always pass them explicitly. * Converters. Self-describing metadata (grid, units, time axis) exist only via npy2nc.py. The checkpoint and reuse_<k>.bin record files are not converted to .npy. * Build portability. Only the macOS / Apple-silicon configuration of Installation has been tested; the non-conda (FFTW_PREFIX) and OpenBLAS paths have not. * Anderson mixing, the secant outer update and the --reuse variants other than warm are experimental and were not used in the paper. * The example scripts in examples/ are templates for the benchmark cases; they expect the input trees produced by the scripts in tools/.

docs.title: Checks made during development
docs.text:
These checks were made during development with tools that are not part of this release; they are recorded here and are not meant to be repeated.

Exactness against the legacy solver

  • Run both solvers on the same inputs and configuration with SLEVOLVE_INNER=off and no warm start. The legacy reference build uses the corrected fft99b. The legacy build scripts and the comparison scripts used during development are not part of this release.
  • Pass criteria:
  • final topography differs by < 1e-11 m between exact SLEvolve variants and the legacy solver (binary output);
  • identical numiter at every step;
  • identical ocean and beta masks.
  • Comparisons against legacy text output are limited by the ES16.9E2 print precision (~4e-6 m).

Acceptance criteria used during development

  • Every stage was accepted only after it reproduced the preceding stage numerically on the benchmark cases (paper Sect. 2.8): same inner-iteration counts and masks, and topography within round-off.
  • Switches that only change the iteration start (extrap, warm, T0 guess) were accepted on agreement within epsilon1 and on the converged outer misfit.
  • Fortran and Python are cross-checked against each other.
  • Repeat runs give identical output.

File converters

  • Converters, on one file of each text layout (row-e.18, row-e16.7, row-E18.10):
  • Fortran- and Python-written .npy files are identical.
  • np.load of the Fortran file equals the text parse.
  • text -> npy -> text reproduces the original file exactly in its own format, in both languages.
  • es16.9 output is identical between Fortran and Python and round-trips exactly.
  • The Fortran reader also handles fortran_order=True and |i1 files.
  • Solver, 20 Case 1 steps with all snapshot fields: reading <f4 .npy ice and a <f8 .npy topography gives output identical to reading the headerless .bin caches, and all scalar text outputs are identical (except CPU time).
  • Python, 20 steps, lmax 511: reading the Fortran-written .npy inputs gives output identical to reading the text files; the .npy headers of tgrid, ocean and dS_converged are identical to the Fortran files'.

docs.title: Reproducing the published results
docs.text: This page states which run of the benchmark cases corresponds to which result of the paper and what it should give.

docs.title: Case 1: Antarctic forward run
docs.text:
Expected output

  • RUN_case1/OUTPUT_SLM/tgrid550.npy (Fortran) or OUT_case1_py/tgrid550.npy (Python).
  • Against the archived run: 2.05 m area-weighted RMS on a 12.3 m signal (0.024 m with the shelf-removal initialization mimicked); see Benchmark provenance and paper Sect. 4.4.

Reproduction of the archived output (paper Sect. 4.4). With the total ice, SLEvolve reproduces the archived 550-yr topography to 2.05 m area-weighted RMS on a 12.3 m signal. The residual is the step-1 shelf removal: the archived run let the removed shelves enter the elastic and mass-conservation terms (and the rotational feedback) at step 1 but not the viscous memory. With that initialization mimicked, the agreement is 0.024 m RMS. The legacy code and SLEvolve agree with each other to machine precision (< 1e-11 m) in every configuration.

Python imports. The modules of python/slevolve/ import each other relatively (from .solver import ..., from .. import npyio in slevolve.tools), so the same files work installed (pip install .) and from a checkout. The scripts python/run_ais.py, python/run_outer.py, python/init_topo_segmented.py and python/tools/<name>.py put python/ on sys.path and call main() of the package module, so the documented commands are unchanged. Code outside the package (tests, examples, tools/) imports from the package: from slevolve.solver import LoveNumbers, from slevolve.tools.plot_fields import mollweide_map, after sys.path.insert(0, "python") in a checkout or with no path change when the package is installed. run_ais and run_outer parse their arguments and pin the thread counts at import, before NumPy is imported; import slevolve itself does not import NumPy.

docs.title: 2.1 Modules and build order
docs.text:
build.sh compiles, in this order: the generated support module, npy_io_mod.f90, io_mod.f90, spharmt_otf.f90 (as spharmt.o), modal_state_mod.f90, sl_model_mod.f90 and the selected driver. The use relations are:

driver (run_from_zero_plus | run_outer_plus | run_outer_mem)
 |-- sl_model_mod                      sl_model_mod.f90
 |    |-- spharmt                      spharmt_otf.f90 (+ otf_kernels.inc with SHT=otf)
 |    |-- user_specs_mod               generated support module
 |    |-- planets_mod                  generated support module
 |    |    `-- constants_mod
 |    |-- sl_io_mod                    generated support module (legacy text read_sl / write_sl)
 |    |    `-- user_specs_mod
 |    |-- modal_state_mod              modal_state_mod.f90
 |    `-- io_mod                       io_mod.f90
 |         `-- npy_io_mod              npy_io_mod.f90
 |-- spharmt                           (sht_profile counters)
 |-- user_specs_mod                    (dt1; outer drivers)
 `-- io_mod                            (pp_read_options, pp_shtprof)

Compile-time parameters (step length dt1, number of steps L_sim, truncation norder, tolerance epsilon1, file names, tpw, checkmarine, initial_topo, constants) live in user_specs_mod and are set by build.sh. Run-time switches are environment variables read by io_mod::pp_read_options (with inner_read_options and opt_read_options) and by spharmt::sht_env_init (SLEVOLVE_FFT); see Command-line options.

docs.title: 2.2 Drivers
docs.text:
All three drivers call the same solver routines:

  1. sl_solver_checkpoint(itersl, dtime): checks dtime == dt1, sets the planet (set_planet), reads the run-time options, initialises the transform backend (sht_env_init, spharmt_init).
  2. Step 0: sl_timewindow(0), sl_allocate_and_initialize_array, sl_solver_init(itersl, 0.0), sl_deallocate_array.
  3. Steps iter = 1..LAST: sl_timewindow(iter), sl_allocate_and_initialize_array, sl_solver(itersl, iter, dtime, 0.0), sl_deallocate_array.
  4. sl_print_counts.
driver command what differs run_from_zero_plus.f90 ./exe LAST forward run; itersl = 1, step length dt1 = build-time DT (or the times file); optional transform profile print (SLEVOLVE_SHTPROF) run_outer_plus.f90 ./exe LAST [ITERSL] one outer pass; dtime = dt1; pass ITERSL > 1 reads pred_pres_topo_<k-1> and tgrid0_<k-1> from OUTPUT_SLM/ in sl_solver_init run_outer_mem.f90 ./exe LAST K0 K1 passes K0..K1 in one process; sets pp_mem_outer, reads SLEVOLVE_ICECACHE; calls sl_outer_reset between passes; copies OUTPUT_SLM/numiter to numiter_<k> and prints the wall time per pass

The outer update of the initial topography is done in sl_solver_init at the start of pass itersl > 1 (Picard update, or outer_secant with SLEVOLVE_OUTER=secant). At the last step, sl_solver writes pred_pres_topo_<itersl> and tgrid0_<itersl> (and with run_outer_mem also keeps them in memory for the next pass).

docs.title: 2.3 One time step (sl_model_mod::sl_solver)
docs.text:
1. Setup and ice. opt_setup; the ice grid of the current step is read with pp_ice_get (at iter == 1 also the time-zero grid). pp_ice_get serves the grid from the in-memory ice cache (run_outer_mem) or through pp_read_grid (.npy, then .bin, then text). The physical times of the previous and current step are appended to the time array file.
  2. Step-0 fields. tinit_0, cxy0, beta0 stay resident (re-read only with SLEVOLVE_COMPAT bit 1); the previous step's ocean function is already in cxy.
  3. Earth model (once per run). The Love-number file is parsed in the block "Read in Love numbers", guarded by pp_love_ready; the response spectrum exact_spec (decay rates and the weights a_sl, a_rr, degree-2 a_il, a_m, a_tsl, a_trr, and a_hl, a_thl when SLEVOLVE_HORIZ > 0) is built from it, and exact_state%init allocates the modal state.
  4. Advance-and-read. At iter == 1 the state is zeroed (exact_state%zero); otherwise it is resident (or reloaded with load_checkpoint under SLEVOLVE_COMPAT bit 4). Then exact_state%advance_and_read advances every modal state by one decay factor and returns the viscous sea-level and radial sums and the degree-2 rotational sums. These are frozen for the whole inner iteration. The cumulative loads deltaS(:,:,exact_prev), oldil, oldm and the previous deltalambda are restored from p_ocean, p_il, p_m, p_lambda.
  5. Ice and ocean setup. Transform of the initial topography (once, pp_t0lm_ready), the grounded-ice and beta fields (STEP 3), the warm-start read warm_read (with SLEVOLVE_REUSE=warm; replaces the ocean mask), and the batched analyses (opt_ana_multi) of the ice, cstar and tO grids.
  6. Inner start. Eustatic first guess for the ocean-load increment load_inc_lm; with SLEVOLVE_INNER=extrap (or anderson) and two stored converged increments, the extrapolated start replaces it; with a warm-start record, the stored increment of the previous pass replaces both.
  7. Inner iteration (the do loop between "Start of inner loop" and "End of inner loop"): rotation (tpw: moment of inertia, m, lambda, using the frozen exact_sum_il, exact_sum_m, exact_tsl, exact_trr); sea-level change from the load (STEP 6, elastic part plus frozen viscous); synthesis; r0, conservation term and new ocean load (STEPS 7 to 9); convergence measure xi on sum(abs(load_inc_lm)); ocean-function update and re-analysis while xi > epsilon1; optional Anderson mixing (inner_anderson). The loop exits when xi <= epsilon1 and aborts at 9999 iterations.
  8. After convergence. The converged load_inc_lm and dtime are pushed into the extrapolation history (extrap_dsm1, extrap_dsm2, extrap_dtm1, extrap_dtm2); R and G are formed from the frozen exact_radial when they are written (lazyrg); the optional horizontal read-out (exact_state%read_horizontal, SLEVOLVE_HORIZ) is done on the same states.
  9. Commit. The current load rhoi*dicestar + rhow*load_inc_lm (degrees 1..norder) is added to p_load with exact_state%commit (with dil, dm, dlambda when tpw); the cumulative p_ice, p_ocean, prev_ice are stored; save_checkpoint only with SLEVOLVE_CKPT or SLEVOLVE_COMPAT bit 4.
  10. Topography and outputs. topoxy = tinit - deltaslxy, new ocean function cxy (STEP 11); warm_write (warm-start store); diagnostics (ocean areas, GMSL, ice volume); text scalars (numiter, nmelt, TPW<N>, ...); grids through pp_write_grid (tgrid, ocean, beta, R, G) and pp_write_cplx (dS_converged), subject to SLEVOLVE_SNAP; at the last step pred_pres_topo_<itersl> and tgrid0_<itersl>.

docs.title: 3. Python architecture
docs.text:
run_ais.py (forward)        run_outer.py (outer passes)       init_topo_segmented.py
      |                            |                                 |
      |  npyio (read_grid, IceDir, save_grid, save_spectral)        |  solver.LoveNumbers, Planet
      |  solver.LoveNumbers, Planet                                  |
      |  sht_ducc.make_sht -> sht.SHT | sht_ducc.DuccSHT            |
      v                            v
solver_opt.OptSeaLevelSolver  (subclass of solver.SeaLevelSolver, overrides step)
      |-- state: solver_opt.ExactMemoryFast (subclass of solver.ExactMemory)  [opt "numba"]
      |          or solver.ExactMemory
      |-- kernels (Numba kernels)                                            [opt "numba"]
      |-- solver_opt._Anderson                                               [--inner anderson]
      `-- horiz.gradient (grid components, called by the drivers)            [--horizontal-grid]
  • run_ais.py parses the options, builds the ice cache, reads the topography (read_grid_any) and the Love numbers (solver.LoveNumbers), creates the transform with sht_ducc.make_sht (--sht numpy|ducc), and uses OptSeaLevelSolver when --opt or --inner is given, otherwise the reference SeaLevelSolver (with dt = --dt, or the first step of --times). It then calls step(ice[k]) for k = 1..steps and writes tgrid<k>.npy, ocean, beta, R, G, dS_converged, horiz (--save-fields, --horizontal, --horizontal-grid), numiter.npy and run_log.json.
  • run_outer.py creates one OptSeaLevelSolver per outer pass (dt=--dt, default opt raw,diag,dsl,numba,sums, ducc0 transform), passes the dict store that survives across passes for --reuse warm, runs all steps, and updates the initial topography by Picard or per-cell secant (--outer). It writes pred_pres_topo_<it>.npy, tgrid0_<it>.npy, saved steps and T0_next.npy.
  • solver.SeaLevelSolver.__init__ does what sl_solver_init does (step 0: initial topography, ocean and beta functions, their spectra) and creates the state ExactMemory; OptSeaLevelSolver.__init__ replaces it by ExactMemoryFast when numba is selected.
  • OptSeaLevelSolver.step follows the same sequence as sl_solver: state.advance_and_read(), ice and ocean grids (kernels.icestar_beta_cstar_tO), ice analysis and increments, eustatic guess, extrapolated start (inner != "off"), warm start (reuse_store), inner loop (rotation, kernels.b18, synthesis, conservation, kernels.dS_update, convergence measure xi, ocean-function update or Anderson mixing), history push, R/G from radial, optional horizontal_lm, state.commit(...), topography and ocean function (kernels.topo_ocean), diagnostics. It returns a dict of fields (tgrid, ocean, beta, R, G, dS_converged, horiz, scalars).
  • parse_opts turns --opt (raw, diag, dsl, numba, sums, or all) into a set; each item switches one optimisation of step.
  • sht.SHT (NumPy/BLAS table) and sht_ducc.DuccSHT (ducc0) share analysis(grid, out) and synthesis(coeffs, out); make_sht(backend, ...) selects one. The raw option exists only for ducc0.
  • npyio holds the file conventions shared with the Fortran (read_grid tries .npy, .bin, text; IceDir reads <dir>/<pfx><k> on demand).
  • horiz.gradient(U, nlat, nlon) turns the spectral Psi_lm into (u_theta, u_phi) with the ducc0 spin-1 gradient synthesis.

docs.title: 4.1 Modal-state advance and commit
docs.text:
The advance loop of state_advance_and_read in fortran/src/modal_state_mod.f90 (the degree-2 rotational states follow after it):

call update_decay(self,spec,dt_years)
viscous=(0.0_dp,0.0_dp); radial=(0.0_dp,0.0_dp)

! Packed layout is [degree][pole][m=0:l], so each pole update is one
! contiguous vector operation.  R itself is the hereditary response state:
! R_new = d*R_old + (1-d)*DL_old   (DL = cumulative load, p_load).
! degrees are independent (each writes a disjoint slice of
! r_load / viscous / radial and accumulates over kk in the same order),
! so this loop threads identically.
!$omp parallel do schedule(dynamic,4) default(shared) private(ll,kk,ibase,rstart,rend,d,omd)
do ll=1,self%lmax
   ibase=lm_index(ll,0)
   do kk=1,self%nmod(ll)
      d=self%decay(kk,ll); omd=1.0_dp-d
      rstart=int(self%roffset(ll))+(kk-1)*(ll+1)
      rend=rstart+ll
      self%r_load(rstart:rend)=d*self%r_load(rstart:rend) + &
                                omd*self%p_load(ibase:ibase+ll)
      viscous(ibase:ibase+ll)=viscous(ibase:ibase+ll) + &
                              spec%a_sl(kk,ll)*self%r_load(rstart:rend)
      radial(ibase:ibase+ll)=radial(ibase:ibase+ll) + &
                             spec%a_rr(kk,ll)*self%r_load(rstart:rend)
   end do
end do
!$omp end parallel do

state_commit in the same file only adds the converged increments to the accumulated loads:

subroutine state_commit(self,current_load,dil,dm,dlambda)
  class(response_memory_state), intent(inout) :: self
  complex(dp), intent(in) :: current_load(:)
  real(dp), intent(in), optional :: dil(3,3),dm(3)
  complex(dp), intent(in), optional :: dlambda(0:2)
  self%p_load=self%p_load+current_load
  if (present(dil)) self%p_il=self%p_il+dil
  if (present(dm)) self%p_m=self%p_m+dm
  if (present(dlambda)) self%p_lambda=self%p_lambda+dlambda
end subroutine state_commit

The Python equivalent of the advance, the body of advance_and_read in python/slevolve/kernels.py (state stored as R[l, k, m], used by ExactMemoryFast):

nl = R.shape[0]
for l in prange(nl):
    nk = nmod[l]
    for m in range(nl):
        visc[l, m] = 0.0
        rad[l, m] = 0.0
    for k in range(nk):
        d = decay[k, l]
        o = omd[k, l]
        s = a_sl[k, l]
        q = a_rr[k, l]
        for m in range(l + 1):
            x = R[l, k, m] * d + P[l, m] * o
            R[l, k, m] = x
            visc[l, m] += x * s
            rad[l, m] += x * q

Here P (p_load in both codes) holds the cumulative load ΔL(t_{j-1}).

and ExactMemory.commit in python/slevolve/solver.py:

def commit(self, current_load, dil=None, dm=None, dlambda=None):
    self.p_load += current_load
    if dil is not None:
        self.p_il += dil
    if dm is not None:
        self.p_m += dm
    if dlambda is not None:
        self.p_lambda += dlambda

docs.title: 4.2 Placement of advance and commit in the time step
docs.text:
In sl_solver (fortran/src/sl_model_mod.f90) the state is advanced and read once before the inner iteration and committed once after convergence; the inner iteration and the R, G and horizontal read-outs lie between the two parts (left out):

! the 53 MB hereditary state stays in memory across timesteps;
! the baseline writes and reads it back on every single step.
if (iter == 1) then
   call exact_state%zero()
   pp_state_ready = .true.
else if (.not. pp_state_ready .or. iand(pp_compat,4) /= 0) then
   call exact_state%load_checkpoint(trim(exact_statefile),exact_spec)
   pp_state_ready = .true.
endif
call exact_state%advance_and_read(exact_spec,real(dtime,dp),exact_viscous,exact_radial, &
                                  exact_sum_il,exact_sum_m,exact_tsl,exact_trr)
...
! Commit the converged current-step increments only now.  The current
! load has zero age at this instant, so it did not contribute to the
! hereditary response used above; it becomes memory for future steps.
exact_current_load = (0.0_dp,0.0_dp)
!$omp parallel do schedule(static) default(shared) private(l,m,exact_idx)
do l = 1,norder
   do m = 0,l
      exact_idx = lm_index(l,m)
      exact_current_load(exact_idx) = rhoi*dicestar(l,m,exact_cur) + rhow*load_inc_lm(l,m)
   enddo
enddo
!$omp end parallel do
if (tpw) then
   call exact_state%commit(exact_current_load,dil(:,:,exact_cur),dm(:,exact_cur),dlambda(2,0:2,exact_cur))
else
   call exact_state%commit(exact_current_load)
endif

The same placement in OptSeaLevelSolver.step (python/slevolve/solver_opt.py):

viscous, radial, sum_il, sum_m, exact_tsl, exact_trr = self.state.advance_and_read()
mark("memory", t0)
...

    np.multiply(self.load_inc_lm, p.rhow, out=self._sp2)

docs.title: 4.3 Extrapolated inner start
docs.text:
The coefficients are computed by extrap_coeffs in fortran/src/modal_state_mod.f90; for equal steps they are exactly 2 and -1:

! Coefficients of the extrapolated inner start (variable steps):
!   dS0_j = dt_j [ Sdot_{j-1} + (Sdot_{j-1} - Sdot_{j-2}) (dt_j + dt_{j-1}) / (dt_{j-1} + dt_{j-2}) ],
!   Sdot_i = dS_i / dt_i,   i.e.  dS0_j = c1 dS_{j-1} + c2 dS_{j-2};
! equal steps give exactly c1 = 2, c2 = -1.  dt0 = dt_j, dtm1 = dt_{j-1}, dtm2 = dt_{j-2}.
pure subroutine extrap_coeffs(dt0, dtm1, dtm2, c1, c2)
  real(dp), intent(in) :: dt0, dtm1, dtm2
  real(dp), intent(out) :: c1, c2
  if (dt0 == dtm1 .and. dtm1 == dtm2) then
     c1 = 2.0_dp; c2 = -1.0_dp
  else
     c1 = dt0 / dtm1 * (1.0_dp + (dt0 + dtm1) / (dtm1 + dtm2))
     c2 = -dt0 / dtm2 * ((dt0 + dtm1) / (dtm1 + dtm2))
  endif
end subroutine extrap_coeffs

and applied in sl_solver (fortran/src/sl_model_mod.f90), where dtr is the length of the current step (from the times file, else the build-time DT):

! extrap: linear-in-time extrapolation of the converged
! increment; the cumulative current load that the first rotation
! evaluation reads is made consistent with it.  For uniform steps this
! is 2 dS(n-1) - dS(n-2); for variable steps the rate dS/dt is
! extrapolated linearly between step midpoints and scaled by dt(n).
if (inner_mode > 0) then
   if (.not. allocated(extrap_dsm1)) then
      allocate(extrap_dsm1(0:norder,0:norder), extrap_dsm2(0:norder,0:norder))
      extrap_dsm1 = (0.0,0.0); extrap_dsm2 = (0.0,0.0)
   endif
   if (inner_nhist >= 2) then
      ! paper Sect. 2.5: dS0_j = c1 dS_{j-1} + c2 dS_{j-2} (modal_state_mod::extrap_coeffs)
      call extrap_coeffs(dtr, extrap_dtm1, extrap_dtm2, extrap_c1, extrap_c2)
      !$omp parallel do schedule(static) default(shared) private(m)
      do m = 0,norder
         load_inc_lm(:,m) = extrap_c1 * extrap_dsm1(:,m) + extrap_c2 * extrap_dsm2(:,m)
         deltaS(:,m,exact_cur) = deltaS(:,m,exact_prev) + load_inc_lm(:,m)
      enddo
      !$omp end parallel do
   endif
   inner_nh = 0; inner_lastmixed = .false.; inner_plain_rest = .false.; inner_nrefreeze = 0

The Python version is extrap_guess in python/slevolve/solver_opt.py:

def extrap_guess(h1, h2, dt0, dt1, dt2, out=None):
    """Extrapolated inner start of step j (paper Sect. 2.5):

        dS0_j = dt_j [ Sdot_{j-1} + (Sdot_{j-1} - Sdot_{j-2}) (dt_j + dt_{j-1}) / (dt_{j-1} + dt_{j-2}) ],
        Sdot_i = dS_i / dt_i,

    with h1 = dS_{j-1}, h2 = dS_{j-2}, dt0 = dt_j, dt1 = dt_{j-1}, dt2 = dt_{j-2}.  Equal steps give
    exactly 2 dS_{j-1} - dS_{j-2}."""
    if out is None:
        out = np.empty_like(h1)
    if dt0 == dt1 == dt2:
        np.multiply(h1, 2.0, out=out)
        out -= h2
    else:
        w = (dt0 + dt1) / (dt1 + dt2)
        np.multiply(h1, dt0 / dt1 * (1.0 + w), out=out)
        out -= (dt0 / dt2 * w) * h2
    return out

called in OptSeaLevelSolver.step with the lengths of the current and the two previous steps:

if acc and self._dS_nhist >= 2:
    h1, h2 = self._dS_hist  # dS_{n-1}, dS_{n-2}
    # linear-in-time extrapolation of the increment: for uniform steps
    # 2 dS_{n-1} - dS_{n-2}; for variable steps the rate dS/dt is
    # extrapolated between step midpoints and scaled by dt_n
    extrap_guess(h1, h2, float(self.dt), self._dt_hist[0], self._dt_hist[1],
                 out=self.load_inc_lm)
    # the rotation block of iteration 1 reads deltaS_cur: give it the
    # same guess (plain iteration 1 reads 0 here)
    np.add(deltaS_prev, self.load_inc_lm, out=self.deltaS_cur)

docs.title: 4.4 Love-number file read
docs.text:
The reader in sl_solver (fortran/src/sl_model_mod.f90), executed once per run: one header line, then per degree the number of modes, the decay rates, the elastic and asymptotic lines, and the h, l, k residues, followed for l >= 2 by the same lines for the tidal numbers:

open(unit = 201, file = trim(planetfolder)//trim(planetmodel), status = 'old')
! Reader as in the legacy code of Han et al. (2022)
read(201,*)
do j = 1,norder
   read(201,*) legord(j), nmodes(j)
   nm = nmodes(j)
   xn = real(legord(j))
   ll = legord(j)
   nmod(ll) = nm
   read(201,*) (s(i,ll), i=1, nm)
   read(201,*) elast(1,ll), elast(2,ll), taurr, taurt, elast(3,ll)
   read(201,*) asymv(1,ll), asymv(2,ll), taurr, taurt, asymv(3,ll)
   read(201,*) (resh(i,ll), i=1,nm)
   read(201,*) (resl(i,ll), i=1,nm)
   read(201,*) (resk(i,ll), i=1,nm)
   if (xn .lt. 1.5) cycle
   read(201,*) telast(1,ll), telast(2,ll), dmx, dmy, telast(3,ll)
   read(201,*) tasymv(1,ll), tasymv(2,ll), dmx, dmy, tasymv(3,ll)
   read(201,*) (tresh(i,ll), i=1, nm)
   read(201,*) (tresl(i,ll), i=1, nm)
   read(201,*) (tresk(i,ll), i=1, nm)
enddo
close(201)

solver.LoveNumbers in python/slevolve/solver.py reads the same layout.

docs.title: 4.5 Horizontal-displacement read-out
docs.text:
In sl_solver (fortran/src/sl_model_mod.f90), between the inner iteration and the commit: the modal states are read with the l weights and combined with the elastic l number and the degree-2 rotational term:

call exact_state%read_horizontal(exact_spec, exact_horiz, exact_thl)
hzlm(:,:) = (0.0,0.0)
if (nmelt /= 0) then
   !$omp parallel do schedule(static) default(shared) private(l,m,ttl,exact_idx)
   do l = 1,norder
      ttl = (4.0 * pi * (radius**3)) / (mass * (2.0 * real(l) + 1.0)) ! (eq. B16)
      do m = 0,l
         exact_idx = lm_index(l,m)
         hzlm(l,m) = ttl * (elast(2,l)/real(l)) * (rhoi * deltaicestar(l,m,exact_cur) &
                  & + rhow * deltaS(l,m,exact_prev) + rhow * load_inc_lm(l,m)) &
                  & + ttl * exact_horiz(exact_idx)
      enddo
   enddo
   !$omp end parallel do
   if (tpw .and. norder >= 2) then
      do m = 0,2
         hzlm(2,m) = hzlm(2,m) + ((telast(2,2)/2.0) * (deltalambda(2,m,exact_prev) &
                  & + dlambda(2,m,exact_cur)) + exact_thl(m)) / gacc
      enddo
   endif
endif

The Python version, from SeaLevelSolver.horizontal_lm in python/slevolve/solver.py:

visc_h, thl = st.read_horizontal()
A = p.rhoi * deltaicestar + p.rhow * deltaS_prev
A += p.rhow * load_inc_lm
hz = self._ttlle * A + self._ttl * visc_h
hz[0, :] = 0.0
sg = getattr(self, "_msign", 1.0)
if self.tpw and rot_tot is not None and self.norder >= 2:
    rot = (self.love.lTE[2] * rot_tot + thl) / p.gacc
    rot[1] *= sg
    hz[2, 0:3] += rot
if sg != 1.0:  # raw (sign-free) backend: V = (-1)^m U -> U
    hz[:, 1::2] *= -1.0
return hz

docs.title: Verifying the installation
docs.text:
This page lists the checks you can run, which implementation each covers, and what a passing run prints.

check implementation covered needs time Python tests python tests/run_all.py Python solver numpy (ducc0 optional) about 3 s Fortran test bash tests/test_fortran_python.sh Fortran solver, against the Python solver Fortran toolchain, numpy about 30 s Non-uniform-step Fortran test bash tests/test_fortran_python_vardt.sh Fortran solver with a times file (non-uniform and uniform), against the Python solver Fortran toolchain, numpy about 2 min Fortran-only test bash tests/test_fortran_synthetic.sh Fortran solver and Fortran input generator, against a shipped reference Fortran toolchain only (no Python) about 30 s Benchmark reference check python tests/check_reference.py either solver, on a benchmark case the benchmark data 20-40 s per case

docs.title: Python tests
docs.text:
python tests/run_all.py

Five plain scripts (no pytest), all of the Python solver; the three below, and the two non-uniform-step tests of the next section:

  • test_recursion.py: synthetic modal spectrum (random decay rates and residues) and a random step-wise load history with non-uniform steps; the recursive update of solver.ExactMemory is compared with the explicit history sum for the six viscous terms (relative error < 1e-12).
  • test_sht_roundtrip.py: analysis -> synthesis round trip of a band-limited field on the 512 x 1024 grid at lmax 63 and 511, numpy backend and ducc0 if importable (relative error < 1e-12).
  • test_small_case.py: idealised polar ice cap (up to 1000 m, 14 degrees radius, grown and melted over 8 steps of 1 kyr) on a sloping polar continent and a -4000 m ocean, 128 x 256 grid, lmax 63; the marine check removes the floating cap margin and the shoreline moves. It compares (a) the plain recursive solver, (b) the extrapolated inner start and (c) an explicit full-history evaluation of the viscous terms: (a) vs (c) must agree to < 1e-9 m; (a) vs (b) differ by the inner tolerance only. It also reports the fixed-point residual obtained by applying the ocean-load update once more to the converged iterate (information only: the convergence criterion of the solver, the ratio of Kendall et al. (2005) eq. 83, bounds the change of the coefficient sums between iterations, not this residual).

Expected output (numbers may differ in the last digits on other machines):

== test_recursion.py
test_recursion: 60 non-uniform steps (dt 1.9-1948.3 yr), lmax 12, up to 8 modes: max relative error 7.669e-15  (0.02 s)
test_recursion: PASS
== test_sht_roundtrip.py
...
test_sht_roundtrip: PASS
== test_small_case.py
...
test_small_case: (a) recursive vs (c) explicit history: max |diff| 4.547e-13 m (topography and radial displacement, all steps)
test_small_case: (a) plain vs (b) extrapolated start: max |diff| 7.352e-05 m (max |sea-level change| 205.3 m, ratio 3.6e-07; epsilon1 = 1e-05)
...
test_small_case: PASS
== test_extrap_formula.py
...
test_extrap_formula: PASS
== test_small_case_vardt.py
...
test_small_case_vardt: PASS
== 5/5 passed in 3.2 s

The difference of 7.4e-5 m between (a) and (b) is expected: the two inner iterations start from different first guesses and stop when the change between iterations falls below epsilon1 = 1e-5, so they agree to within that tolerance (a ratio of 3.6e-7 of the signal), not to round-off.

docs.title: Non-uniform time steps (times file)
docs.text:
python tests/run_all.py also runs two tests of the non-uniform-step mode:

  • tests/test_extrap_formula.py feeds a known sequence of increments dS_i and step lengths dt_i (uniform: 1 yr; non-uniform: 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 37.5 yr) through the extrapolated inner start of both solvers (Python solver_opt.extrap_guess; Fortran modal_state_mod::extrap_coeffs, compiled when gfortran works, otherwise skipped with a message) and compares with dS0_j = dt_j [Sdot_(j-1) + (Sdot_(j-1) - Sdot_(j-2)) (dt_j + dt_(j-1)) / (dt_(j-1) + dt_(j-2))], Sdot_i = dS_i / dt_i, evaluated independently; equal steps must give exactly 2 dS_(j-1) - dS_(j-2).
  • tests/test_small_case_vardt.py runs the idealised polar ice cap of test_small_case.py with the steps 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 yr from a times file and compares the recursive solver with an explicit full-history sum over the actual times (1e-9 m); it checks that the extrapolated start receives (dt_j, dt_(j-1), dt_(j-2)) from step 3 on, and that a uniform times file reproduces the run without one exactly.
test_extrap_formula: Python extrap_guess vs formula: max relative error 2.216e-16
test_extrap_formula: Fortran extrap_coeffs vs formula: max relative error 2.216e-16
test_extrap_formula: PASS
test_small_case_vardt: (a) recursive vs (c) explicit history: max |diff| 4.547e-13 m (topography and radial displacement, all steps; max |sea-level change| 68.5 m)
test_small_case_vardt: (d) uniform times file vs no times file: max |diff| (a) 0.0 m, (b) 0.0 m
test_small_case_vardt: PASS

Fortran is built with DT unset and finds the file at INPUT_FILES/others/times; Python gets --times. It also runs both solvers with a uniform times file (t_k = k yr; Fortran through SLEVOLVE_TIMES=<file>) and without one. About two minutes.

docs.title: Benchmark reference check
docs.text:
reference/ holds reference results of the three benchmark cases, computed with the Python solver (ducc0 backend, --opt all --inner extrap, --lmax 511, 8 threads, Apple M4 Max). tests/check_reference.py compares a run of either solver with them; it needs the prepared input data of the case (Running the benchmark cases, which also shows maps of the reference results).

  • reference/<case>.json: the area-weighted RMS and max |value| of each stored field, its value at 20 named sites, the number of inner iterations of every step and, for Cases 2 and 3, the outer misfit (area-weighted RMS of T_pred - T_obs) per pass.
  • reference/<case>/*.npy: the full 512 x 1024 fields (<f8):
Case Fields Selected steps 1 dtopo_k = topography change since step 0; dsl_k = relative sea-level change -(topography change) on the ocean of step k 1, 100, 550 2 dtopo_k = topography change since the start of the pass 1, 600, 1200 3 dtopo_p1_s50, dtopo_p5_s50 = topography change at step 50 of passes 1 and 5; T0_minus_obs = converged initial topography (pass 5) minus T_obs 50

Check a finished run:

python tests/check_reference.py --case case1 --dir OUT_case1_py              # Python run
python tests/check_reference.py --case case1 --dir RUN_case1/OUTPUT_SLM      # Fortran run
python tests/check_reference.py --case case3 --dir OUT_case3_py --topo-pres $INPUT3/others/topo_pres

or let it run the reference configuration with the Python solver first and then compare:

python tests/check_reference.py --case case1 --run --input $INPUT1 --workdir RUN

It prints one line per quantity (max |difference| and area-weighted RMS difference of each full field, the RMS and max summaries, the worst site, the inner-iteration counts, the outer misfits) and ends with check_reference case1: PASS, or FAIL and the quantities that differ (exit status 1). Reference fields whose files are not in the run directory are reported as SKIP and listed at the end. The Fortran Case 1 example writes only tgrid0 (the initial topography snapshot) and tgrid550, so dtopo_550 and the iteration counts (from OUTPUT_SLM/numiter) are compared; on the tested machine this gives dtopo_550 max |diff| 8.2e-12 m, identical iteration counts (2099 in all) and check_reference case1: PASS, 5 item(s) skipped.

Tolerances. The default tolerance is 1e-6 m (--tol) for every field and summary, and identical inner-iteration counts (--iter-slack 0). A rerun on the same machine reproduces every field exactly. On other hardware, BLAS libraries or thread counts the round-off differs, a few steps may need one inner iteration more or less, and the fields then differ within the inner tolerance; use --tol 1e-3 --iter-slack 1 there.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
This page defines the terms used throughout the manual.

  • Topography T (tgrid): bedrock elevation relative to the sea surface, m, positive up; the ocean is where T < 0. Relative sea-level change is minus the change of T. All output fields are defined in Output fields.
  • Ocean function C (ocean): 1 where T < 0, else 0. beta (beta): 1 where the cell is free of ice, else 0. The water load sits on C * beta.
  • Marine check (checkmarine): ice on a cell with initial topography T0 <= 0 counts as load only if it is grounded, rhoi * H > rhow * |T0| (920 and 1000 kg m^-3).
  • Inner iteration: at each step, the ocean-load increment is updated until the ocean load, the deformation, the gravity field and the ocean function are consistent. epsilon1 is its stopping tolerance, a dimensionless ratio (Kendall et al. 2005, eq. 83): with S_i the sum of the absolute values of the spherical-harmonic coefficients of the ocean-load increment at iteration i, the loop stops when |S_i - S_(i-1)| / S_(i-1) <= epsilon1 (default 1e-5). It is not a length in metres.
  • Outer iteration (ice age runs): repeats the whole run with an updated initial topography until the predicted present topography matches the observed one. The number of passes is set by the user (run_outer.py --iters, ./exe LAST K0 K1); the Fortran parameter epsilon2 is defined but not used by the code.
  • calcRG: also compute the radial displacement R and the sea-surface change G (R<N>, G<N>).
  • TPW: rotational feedback (true polar wander).

Next: Method overview.
